speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: BARGAINING AND OTHER RIGHTS OF CIVIL SERVANTS- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even though this is a day on which all of us believe a budget will be announced, we do not want to lose sight of the public service. I therefore rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity to bring to the attention of the House, for immediate action, the deeply-aroused and justifiable fear among members of the public service arising out of the deliberate and drastic actions of the government which indicate that the rights of the public service to collective bargaining are in jeopardy.
I would, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen):
That this House declares its unequivocal support of existing undiminished bargaining rights for members of the public service, and protests the right of the government to assign or change duties of public servants, for such would end the classification standards and thereby reduce the merit system.
Furthermore, it protests and condemns the announced policy of the government as being discriminatory and unjust in that the ending shortly of wage and salary controls will not apply to the public service.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS BY AMERICAN MOTORS CORPORATION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, following press reports of a few days ago that the American Motors Corporation will be laying off some 1,000 people on a temporary basis this summer and about 350 people on a permanent basis, all at its
Brampton plant. In light of the fact that since 1974, American Motors has received the benefit of just under $18 million in remissions of duty payable on its car imports, having failed to meet the conditions of the auto pact with respect to production and jobs, all of which duty remissions have been passed by cabinet as orders in council, and since these latest lay-offs mean that American Motors will be even further away from meeting its commitments under the pact, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce be instructed to make a full report before this House as soon as possible of all discussions between his department and American Motors regarding the impact of these lay-offs, of what commitments his department has obtained from American Motors to get employment back up to reasonable levels in Brampton, and what sanctions the government is prepared to take against American Motors in light of its continued failure to meet employment commitments under the auto pact at its Brampton plant.

speechtext:
Perhaps I might take a moment, prior to beginning the question period-I will extend the question

April 3, 1978

period by a minute or two, if I take that long-to inform the House of something. The initial action of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) some weeks ago, followed by similar information given to me by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), respecting the presence of electronic devices in their offices caused me, after consultation with representatives of all parties, to request an investigation by the Ottawa police force. Hon. members will now know that that investigation has resulted in charges which were laid last week.
During the course of those investigations, I sought interim reports only by way of confirmation from the police that investigations were ongoing. I did not request any formal or written reports. I presume that had no conclusive actions resulted from those investigations, probably I would have asked for some sort of report which I would have passed on to the House. In any case, last week when I was out of the country, the Ottawa police force endeavoured to inform me of their intention to proceed with these charges. Being unable to reach me, they contacted the Clerk of the House, who reached me, and after discussion I advised the office of the Prime Minister and the office of the Leader of the Opposition through the Clerk of the House.
I completed the consultative process this morning by advising representatives of all parties of the actions that had been taken by the police, and as this matter is before the courts, I would not propose to seek a report of any sort from the police. In fact, I was informed later today-just before coming to the House-that if I were to do so, I could not really receive much more information than is publicly known, that is, that the investigations have led to the laying of charges and that these charges are now before the courts.
In the circumstances, I do not propose to pursue the matter any further. I will simply make a statement, after consultation with representatives of all parties, so the House is fully informed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. A short while ago the Prime Minister spoke to the Economic Club of New York. During that speech he said "the recovery is under way": he was referring to Canada. Canadians were amazed to discover it, of course. Since unemployment currently registers officially at one million, and unofficially at 1.6 million, since investment intentions for 1978, according to the Minister of Finance, are worse than they were for 1977, since the dollar dropped 24 hours after the Prime Minister made his speech, and continues to drop, I ask the Prime Minister most seriously why he misinformed his American audience and, more importantly, why he misinformed Canadians who were watching that television performance? Can he cite one economic indicator which would substantiate his absurd claim?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INFORMATION ON ECONOMIC SITUATION GIVEN TO U.S. AUDIENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party is asking for one indicator, I will give him one or two. In the year 1977 there was a marked decline in domestic inflationary pressures. There was significant improvement in the trade balance as the year progressed, and a revival in corporate profits. Real exports rose by 7.7 per cent over 1976 levels, for a second year of strong improvement, while imports dropped only 2 per cent over 1976 levels, for a second year of strong improvement. Therefore, there was a strengthening in the last part of 1977.

That is why I am saying that the trend is toward an optimistic outlook.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, March 22, consideration of Bill C-25, to establish the Northern Pipeline Agency, to facilitate the planning and construction of a pipeline for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska and Northern Canada and to give effect to an Agreement between Canada and the United States of America on principles applicable to such a pipeline and to amend certain acts in relation thereto, as reported (with amendments) from the Special Committee on a Northern Gas Pipeline. subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to welcome back to the House the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) who was not with us on Tuesday, March 21, and Wednesday, March 22, when a major portion of these amendments was debated.
The minister's colleagues missed his presence. It is a pity that he was not here because the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who attended the majority of the committee meetings, seemed to have left his responsibilities to the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), who advanced some rather empty, unintelligent, and innocuous amendments.
The amendments we were dealing with at the time of adjournment were motions Nos. 4 and 6 with respect to the injection of a native presence into the bill. I had made a few remarks with respect to the representations made by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, but before I terminate my brief remarks I want to correct a mistaken impression which appears to have been held by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Milne). As stated by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent

(Mr. Holmes), we on this side wanted to see a stronger amendment in the bill with respect to the native presence than that which is now set forth in motion No. 6. We wanted to see two elements in that amendment. We wanted to see, first, that the land which would be occupied along the route of the pipeline would be treated in such a manner that any existing native claims would not be prejudiced by that occupation.
Secondly, and equally as important, we wanted to reassure the native peoples that their ongoing negotiations toward a final settlement would not be prejudiced by the bill itself.
The first of those elements is in the amendment which the government has accepted. The second of those elements is not present. We settled on the basis of getting this much from the government. We would have liked to have seen the other element contained in the amendment. With those words 1 intend to leave the amendments with respect to native peoples. I believe that the amendment which the government finally did accept, as set forth in motion No. 6, adequately protects native interests not only in the Yukon but also in northern British Columbia as well as any which may exist in Alberta with respect to any interest the native peoples may have in the land on which the pipeline will be located. That, to my mind, covers the situation as far as the land itself is concerned, and adequately protects native claims. There was no such protection before, but this amendment will provide it.
I would like to say one last word about the position taken by the NDP. In essence it reflects the position which is being taken by the representations of the native people themselves. Members of the NDP say that there should be no development whatsoever until native claims are settled. The native organizations say there should be no development until their claims are settled. To my mind that is a totally irresponsible position to be taking.
Out of one side of their mouths members of the NDP are saying that we need jobs in Canada. They criticize the government, as we do, for bringing about a situation where there is in excess of one million unemployed, yet out of the other side of their mouths they try to throw up a roadblock by saying that there should be no pipeline whatsoever until native land claims are settled. They thereby would throw down the drain 100,000 man-years of employment.
It seems to me that members of the NDP cannot have it both ways. That is why, before the adjournment, I referred to them as being rather sanctimonious. It is quite a hypocritical stand for them to be taking. It is hypocritical to say that there should not be this development, thus dispensing effectively with the jobs they criticize the government for not creating. The stance of my party, as expressed by my leader repeatedly, is that there is no reason why negotiations for settlement of native claims cannot proceed hand in hand with any development, including the pipeline, without the one prejudicing the other.
No one has been able to convince me yet-and I invite members of the NDP to try-that the building of a pipeline would prejudice native land claims. No one has yet been able to convince me that the building of a road, the building of a
April 3, 1978

bridge, or the bringing into being of a new mine would be prejudicial to the settlement of native land claims. 1 invite members of the NDP to tell me how they feel this would happen. It just would not happen at all.
Native peoples negotiate on the basis of land, cash, royalties and so forth. Whatever land is to be occupied by the development of a new mine can be negotiated on the basis of royalties. That has been done elsewhere in this country, and elsewhere in the western world where native land claims have been settled. There is no reason why that cannot be done here. In his ignorance of the Yukon the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie does not realize that 90 per cent of the native people in the Yukon do not share the views expressed by their leaders down here when they appear before committees. The Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) is listening very carefully, and he knows what I say is true. Millions of dollars are poured into the support of native organizations, which are headed by bureaucrats.
Since 1973 well over $40 million or $50 million has been poured into native organizations in the Yukon, yet the kids in Pelly Crossing, Ross River Upper Liard and other native Yukon communities are still running around with no jeans on their backsides. So one wonders where the money goes, particularly when one legal counsel is paid $95,000 a year for a great many years. The present legal counsel is being paid $65,000 a year, and he was just appointed last June.
One wonders whether these moneys are being properly spent. The native people of the Yukon are not seeing the benefits. If they would come to an agreement in principle and pick up the $50 million which is now lying on the table waiting for them to pick up, they would be ready and capable of being part of the economic activity and development which will take place as part of the pipeline. However, instead of taking that sensible course, the result of the course they are taking is the loss of $400,000 a month in interest on that money. The economic and social conditions which exist in their villages throughout the Yukon will continue to exist while they adopt that dog-in-the-manger attitude.
It does them no good, it does the country no good, and it does the Yukon as a whole no good for any segment of the population anywhere along that line to adopt the attitude that they will prevent a project of such magnitude-a project that would bring about national benefits-for the sake of having a lever for the purpose of bringing about what they think will be a favourable settlement. On the contrary, it is in their best interest, just as it is in the national best interest and in the over-all best interest of the Yukon, to see that this project goes ahead without prejudice to the final settlement of their native land claims.
With those words stating our position on the matter I will leave those amendments, Mr. Speaker.

Marie. If he were here today-I think he will be here later on this afternoon-he would be making arguments on precisely the same lines as those made by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie.
I am surprised that the hon. member for Yukon, who professes to be interested in the welfare of the native people of this country, should express surprise that we raise issues which are of concern to the native people. He has native people in his constituency, and he must know that the native people in his constituency, as in every other area of this country, have consistently been ignored, that whether one looks at the standards of education, the standards of health or standards of employment, the native people are at the bottom of the heap.
The infant mortality rate of native people is dramatically higher than that of any other group in this country; the educational attainments of the native people over the years have improved but they are still at the bottom of the totem pole, and the employment of native people is still worst of any group in this country. In the cities of Canada they find it almost impossible to find employment, and on the reserves unemployment runs at anywhere from 50 per cent to 95 per cent.
It is not surprising, therefore, that native people have been very suspicious-not just the native people in the Yukon but those in every part of Canada-of the supposed good intentions of the white people and of both the federal and provincial governments. It is not surprising, because they have had such bad experiences in the past. They know that the agreements

April 3, 1978
Northern Pipeline
and treaties have simply not been lived up to, and certainly have not been amended or changed to meet their needs in modern times. They have not been changed so that the spirit, which was supposedly contained in the treaties when they were originally signed, has any meaning in modern times.
Based on the experience of the native people in all parts of Canada, and based on the history of Canada, we have come to the conclusion-and we know we are right-that should the pipeline be proceeded with and should all the details, except those pertaining to native land claims, be proceeded with and the pipeline begun, the chances of the native people of the Yukon getting a fair and equitable settlement are virtually nil.
I suggest to the hon. member for Yukon that when he proposes, as he did consistently in his speech, that the pipeline be proceeded with immediately and the question of native land claims settled later, what he is saying in fact is that the native land claims are not important and that they would be settled probably at 2 cents on the dollar after the project has begun. That is the only clout which the native people of the Yukon have, and we saw a dramatic example of just how this works with regard to the James Bay claims.
Does the hon. member for Yukon really believe that if the native people of James Bay had not gone to court and had not been able to get a court order holding up the James Bay project, they would have achieved the kind of settlement which they got? There is not a chance in the world that that would have happened. If the James Bay people got a settlement which goes at least part way toward meeting their fair claims and which gives them the right to exclusive use of a fairly large piece of land in their ancestral homeground, if they got a large amount of money which will be used to help them develop alternative methods of employment, it is because they had the power, through the courts before the project was completed, of holding up the project. So when the hon. member for the Yukon says that we should leave this issue until later and go ahead with the project right now, what he is saying is that this project is so important to the non-native people of Canada that we must go ahead with it right away, and in doing so he is prepared to sacrifice the basic rights and needs of the native people of this country. We are not prepared to do that.
The hon. member for Yukon knows full well that no one in the NDP has tried to hold up the passage of this bill. He knows that this bill will pass in this session of parliament; it will probably be passed in the next few days. So when he says that we are prepared to stop this bill, he knows that what he is saying is not in fact correct. First of all, to put the case of the native people in the way in which it has not been done, certainly by the hon. member for the Yukon, I have a feeling he may not be speaking for all members of the Conservative party. Certainly he did not put the case for the native people, particularly those in his own constituency. By moving this amendment, we are attempting to provide the House with a clear opportunity to vote on a proposal suggesting that this project should not be proceeded with until the native land claims have been settled.
If the government is prepared to deal with native land claims in the Yukon in a fair and equitable manner, surely it should not be difficult to reach an agreement. The manner in which the government has blown hot and cold over the years on the question of native land claims is what bothers me. I put some questions on the order paper last October. They were not answered until a couple of weeks ago. At that time we saw how generously the lawyers who have acted for the native groups in the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, northern Manitoba and the James Bay area have been treated. They have been paid hundreds of thousands-millions of dollars-to act on behalf of native people in the courts in an attempt to protect their rights. I commend the government for that. I think the government should have done that, and I am glad it was done. The government then turned around and appointed people to negotiate on behalf of the government with native people. My experience indicates that the people appointed have very little sympathy for the rights and needs of native people. 1 am talking about the former cabinet minister, for example, who will be negotiating with the native people in the Northwest Territories. The government has blown hot and cold on this entire question of dealing with native people, their rights, and an equitable settlement in the near future.
No land claim settlement will jeopardize the construction of the pipeline. Failure to settle the land claims will create financing problems. Until there is a settlement, and as long as native people have the right to go to court in an attempt to block the construction of the project, as they did in James Bay, no financial institution will be willing to lend money to the pipeline construction, because they will not know when the project will begin, when it will be constructed finally, nor when the gas will move down the pipeline to the United States. The sales of gas to the United States will enable the companies involved to commence paying back the money which they borrowed for the construction.
This amendment will not hold up the construction of the pipeline. On the contrary, we are attempting to ensure that when the bill is passed there will be no difficulties created, nor will legal delays be possible which would postpone construction and place the entire project in jeopardy. We are attempting to guarantee native people that their land claims will be settled before the project goes ahead. It would be a guarantee to native people, as well as telling the government to get off its rear end and begin to negotiate seriously. We do not need the type of procrastination which we have experienced again and again. So-called negotiations have gone on from generation to generation, and not just for a year or two.
We urge hon. members to support this amendment. We feel it will make the bill stronger rather than weaker. Also it will facilitate the construction of the pipeline, rather than hold it up.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cyril Symes (Sault Ste. Marie) moved:
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Motion No. 8.
That Bill C-25, An Act to establish the Northern Pipeline Agency, to facilitate the planning and construction of a pipeline for the transmission of
Northern Pipeline
natural gas from Alaska and Northern Canada and to give effect to an Agreement between Canada and the United States of America on principles applicable to such a pipeline and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, be amended in Schedule III at page 51 by striking out the third line of paragraph 9(a) and substituting the following therefor:
"plan consistent with paragraphs 3(e) and 3(/) and particularly sub-clause 21 (2) of this Act designed to guarantee the maximum possible use of'.
Motion No. 9.
That Bill C-25, An Act to establish the Northern Pipeline Agency, to facilitate the planning and construction of a pipeline for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska and Northern Canada and to give effect to an Agreement between Canada and the United States of America on principles applicable to such a pipeline and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, be amended in Schedule III at page 51 by
(a)	striking out lines 1 to 3 of paragraph 10(a) and substituting the following therefor:
"(a) the company shall design a program consistent with paragraphs 3(e) and 3(J) and particularly sub-clause 21(2) of this Act for the procurement of all goods and services for the pipeline that guarantees that"
(b)	deleting sub-paragraphs 10(a)(i) and 10(a)(ii) and substituting the following therefor:
"(i) where productive capacity exists in Canada preference will be given to Canadian sources in the procurement of such goods and services and their constituent components,
(ii) the level of Canadian content is at least 90 per cent with respect to the origin of products, services and their constituent components,".
Motion No. 10.
That Bill C-25, An Act to establish the Northern Pipeline Agency, to facilitate the planning and construction of a pipeline for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska and Northern Canada and to give effect to an Agreement between Canada and the United States of America on principles applicable to such a pipeline and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, be amended in Schedule III at page 52 by striking out the last line of sub-paragraph 10(h)(ii) and substituting the following therefor:
"trade practices such as dumping, direct and indirect industrial subsidies, transportation subsidies and special tax incentives;".
He said: Mr. Speaker, motions Nos. 8, 9 and 10 standing in my name relate to the question of maximizing and guaranteeing Canadian content in the northern pipeline project. Motion No. 8 seeks to maximize and guarantee the Canadian labour content of the project. Motion No. 9 seeks to maximize and guarantee Canadian content in the pipeline itself, the steel and all other associated projects. Motion No. 10 seeks to define unfair trade practices for clarification, and to strengthen the bill before us so we will not have Canadian companies facing unfair foreign competition when bidding for contracts on this great project.
I should like to deal briefly with motion No. 8, because motion No. 9 is the most substantive and everything else relates to it. The labour content will, of course, relate to the material content of the pipeline.
Given the high state of unemployment in this country, with 1 million officially out of work, but with real unemployment, taking into account hidden unemployment, being somewhere around 1.5 million to 1.6 million, surely we should ensure that this project to build this pipeline from the Alaska gas fields through Canada to the United States provides the maximum possible employment for Canadian labour.

April 3, 1978
Northern Pipeline
As I said before, the pipeline traverses Canadian territory, but in the foreseeable future we will not be deriving benefits from the natural gas flowing through it. Indeed, we will have to rely at some future date on the construction of the Dempster lateral, if and when it is built. In return for giving our American friends this land bridge to move their gas to their southern markets, surely it is not unreasonable to expect that we should get the maximum labour and material content in respect of this project.
The reason we are moving the amendments is that despite the assurances of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mac-Eachen) that we are going to have 100,000 man-years of employment, we are suspicious that this actually will be the case. The reasons for our suspicion were outlined at the second reading stage and I do not have to go into them at this time in great detail.
There are a number of points that should be remembered. First, the guarantee of the Deputy Prime Minister is verbal. It is nowhere stated in the legislation, and it can change as ministers, governments, or what have you change. For this reason we want to take the Deputy Prime Minister at his word and include in the legislation some of the concepts and figures he has given in this House. We have found in the past that what we had been promised by the Liberal government one day has not necessarily turned out to be the case a few months later.
We are also concerned that we will not get the 100,000 man-years promised by the Deputy Prime Minister. If one looks at the various reports put out by both U.S. and Canadian government departments estimating man-years, one will find quite a discrepancy. The company, in testimony before the National Energy Board, gave different figures. We find, for example, that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion commissioned a study on the pipeline and manpower, and concluded that unless we have guarantees written into the legislation, such as proposed by the NDP in its motions, we will not have 100,000 man-years of employment as promised by the Deputy Prime Minister, but something more like 67,000 man-years.
In addition, I referred to examples of United States government departments which also are very optimistic that the United States will get a high proportion of the labour content of this pipeline. They pretty well exclude all Canadian labour on the Alaska portion. The estimates in the United States are that the maximum we can get is about 3 per cent Canadian employment on that section of the line, and virtually nil in respect of the other portion in the United States.
We all remember, of course, that the United States has very many skilled pipeline labourers from the Alaskan, Alyeska Pipeline project available and ready to move in, if and when the opportunity arises. I know there is to be a monitoring agency in an attempt to maximize jobs for people in those areas through which the pipeline will be running, but we all know that the economic determinant here is skilled labour, and that much of that skilled labour is American.
My concern is that unless we have some very strong legislative guarantees we will not have the kind of man-years of employment promised again and again by the Deputy Prime Minister. We are supported in this, for example, by a department of this government, namely, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I would also refer to a report put out by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce of this government, entitled "Canadian Industrial and Manpower Requirements and Content for a Northern Gas Pipeline." This was an analysis published on February 24, 1978. It looks at various pipeline applications at the time; Arctic Gas and Alcan as well. At page 22 of this report it is stated:
The study indicates that most, if not all, of the manpower requirements can be met in Canada. The Department of Manpower and Immigration has presented a policy statement to the Pipeline Commissioner to reflect the objective of 100 per cent Canadian labour sourcing. However, should foreign labour sourcing be necessary, care would have to be taken to ensure that Canadian worker content is optimized. In addition, it may be necessary to develop mechanisms to deal with a possible "spillover" of Alaska wage rates into the Canadian labour sector.
The report of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce indicates that we do have the labour available and, if given a fair chance, we can ensure: that Canadians get the jobs.
In addition, the same report notes at page 7:
It should be noted that apparent pressures from U.S.A. sources have caused Alcan to engage separate U.S.A. engineering management firms for the Alaska portion of the line despite the obvious efficiency of using the Canadian engineering team already assembled.
That gives rise to my concern that we are going to face a lot of pressure from Americans when both the bidding and construction get under way. There will be pressure to have American skilled labour used to the greatest extent possible on this pipeline project. For this reason we should strengthen every clause in the bill that supposedly assures us we will have maximum Canadian labour content.
Motion No. 8 strengthens the verbal commitment of the Deputy Prime Minister by the wording in the legislation.
Motion No. 9 deals with Canadian content, and seeks to again obtain hard, written guarantees in the legislation, particularly if we are going to have maximum Canadian content including steel, valve, and other industrial components.
To begin with I should like to examine what spokesmen for Foothills, the company that is to build this vast project, have said before the National Energy Board. In undertakings given in testimony before the National Energy Board, Foothills promised compliance in certain respects. At page 6D3 it is stated:
The Applicant believes this policy of "Canadian Goods and Services First" will be in the best long term interest of all Canadians because:
1.	The expertise gained by industry and the workmen involved will remain in Canada and will be available for future projects within Canada. In addition, this knowledge will provide a valuable commodity for export to countries in a less favoured position.
2.	The expanded facilities and capability will provide Canada with a more diversified and stable industrial sector.
3.	The Canadian purchases will produce positive employment and economic impact on the regional areas where the goods are produced.
[Mr. Symes.J
April 3, 1978

I am sure my colleague in Cape Breton-East Richmond is very concerned about the regional spin-offs of such a pipeline construction in the steel industry.
4.	A significant portion of the incomes generated by purchases of Canadian goods and services will be spent in Canada, generating further economic benefits. There will also be, because of import substitution, a positive effect on the balance of trade.
So, here was Foothills before the National Energy Board arguing that maximizing Canadian content of this project would have beneficial spinoffs in all areas of the Canadian economy, and we agree. That is why we would like to see some of the promises and undertakings before the NEB reinforced in this legislation that is before us. When it is left to wording such as maximize or optimize and so on, the whole percentage content can vary quite dramatically, and that is why I would like to see some specifics. In my motion I suggest that at least 90 per cent, as the Deputy Prime Minister has said on many occasions, of the content of the pipeline should be Canadian.
We are confident that on a competitive basis, and with that 90 per cent guarantee, there would be no price gouging, and certainly the amendment that we moved earlier, which was unfortunately ruled out of order, was to ensure that. In light of the guarantee, if there was any kind of exorbitant increase in prices, then the government would, of course, have the option of accepting bids outside Canada or from non-Canadian producers. Indeed, as I understand the treaty, that is still the case.
The treaty calls for competitive bidding and probably it would take precedence over some sections of the legislation before us. The fact that Foothills has said it would be a benefit and has given a kind of commitment that it will try to maximize Canadian content for us, is not quite good enough. We want to see that guarantee in the legislation. And why so? Looking at so many of the background reports that have been done on this pipeline, one gets the uneasy feeling that we may end up with less than the Deputy Prime Minister has been promising us. I refer to the report done by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, on page 3:
Given that American firms are very well placed to win contracts for the U.S.A. portions, they, as a result, are in a more favourable position to bid on contracts for the Canadian segment by being able to pass on to the pipeline contractor some portions of the savings to be achieved by combining the Canadian requirements with their existing production for the U.S.A. sections of the line.
Here is another government report which analyses the situation and raises the concern that without these kinds of guarantees there is a natural advantage to the American contractors and bidders.
And again from the same report on page 5:
The danger that sales contracts of Canadian branch plants of foreign multinationals which exceeded their existing capacity would simply be transferred to the non-Canadian parent instead of to alternative Canadian suppliers. Similar problems could occur if the low cost offshore plants were to be used to fill a bid made and originally intended for the successful Canadian subsidiary.
Here is another concern that, because of the branch-plant nature of our economy, if a subsidiary of an American company or any other company could not meet the requirements of the orders, rather than a Canadian company getting the surplus work it would be transferred to a parent company of
Northern Pipeline
that subsidiary. In other words, the possibility of diminishing Canadian content exists. It is a reality and has been acknowledged by a department of this government.
From the same report I point out on page 9, which deals with the pipeline itself:
Competition in world markets is intense and Canadian companies could be outbid by the pricing strategies of Japanese and European pipe producers. Projections by steel experts reflect a tough world competitive situation.
Again, we are committed to accepting bids on a world-wide basis, and we know-I will get into this when I move to my motion No. 10-that they are all unfair trading practices that foreign governments use with their industry to bring the cost of steel pipe below actual costs of production. If that happens, our steel manufacturers will be at a competitive disadvantage. They will not be able to meet these foreign bids. My fear is that there is no mechanism provided to stop that from going on. That is why I want this amendment in the bill.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce study and report concerns me because it looks at the matter of pipe fittings and concludes that there may be difficulty in maximizing Canadian content. They state at page 10 of their report:
The Canadian supply market for pipe fittings has been dominated historically by wholesalers, who distribute imports mainly from Japan and the U.S.A., and distributing subsidiaries of large U.S. producers. These latter subsidiaries have historically procured the rough product from their U.S. parents and only minor additional value is added in Canada. If this situation is not to be perpetuated, it must be clearly stated that Canada expects a high Canadian content for pipe fittings manufacture, at least for the Canadian sections.
Going to page 11 it states:
Unless some form of initiatives in Canadian policy are taken there will be a great temptation to procure pipe fittings from abroad, especially low-priced imports from Japan.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, the studies that have gone on indicate that we should be concerned with maximizing Canadian content, and my amendment will guarantee us that maximizing that we all want.
When we look at the Foothills undertaking before the National Energy Board, they state on page 6D-2 under "Project Procurement":
The Applicant will purchase goods and services from sellers who provide the best combination of price, delivery, service and quality. This normal commercial purchasing criteria will, however, be specifically tempered by the policy which one of the Applicant's sponsor companies (The Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company Limited) has historically followed. This policy is one "where a sufficient number of qualifying Canadian sellers are available to provide competitive quotes, AGTL will limit its bid list to Canadian suppliers.'' When bids must be solicited from non-Canadian sources, the policy is to "buy Canadian" whenever the order can so be filled, and when price is reasonably competitive.
Again, Foothills is in agreement with the kind of amendment that I am putting forward, if one believes the testimony given before the National Energy Board.
Canada has the capability to produce the material content. We have the skilled labour. Surely this will be a great boost, not only in the short-term but in the long-term, for our manufacturing sector which has declined so badly in the past decade. It should be a great chance to regain some lost
4076

April 3, 1978
Northern Pipeline
business. This is why we say it should be put in the legislation to maximize the Canadian content.
Let us say, as I do in my amendment, that we have the 90 per cent figure as the Deputy Prime Minister is so fond of telling us. I know the argument he has advanced in committee and in this House-that we cannot put these guarantees into the legislation because that would contravene the GATT. I thought that this pipeline agreement was a bilateral agreement between Canada and the United States, like other bilateral agreements we have had in the past. I think of the auto pact. Surely under this circumstance we are not bound by the GATT agreement. This is a joint energy undertaking and therefore, in light of the fact that we are providing a land bridge, it is quite normal and reasonable that we should expect domestic content in the construction materials and labour used in the pipeline.
The report of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce notes precedents on pages 35 and 36 in respect of pipeline construction. The last paragraph on page 35 reads as follows:
At the time the Alyeska pipeline was built, it was made clear to several Canadian suppliers that they would have little chance in obtaining contracts for U.S.A. business if similar goods could be obtained in the U.S.A. In fact, ATCO prefab buildings were the only significant Canadian item imported. Similar reports are now being heard vis-a-vis the U.S.A. portions of this pipeline. It should be recalled that significant portions of the Trans-Canada gas pipeline and of two major oil pipelines supplying the Canadian market (the Interprovincial and the Portland-Montreal pipeline) are located in the U.S.A. These portions were built by U.S. management and manpower using primarily U.S. equipment and supplies. Even today, tariffs continue to be paid in the U.S. on the movement of Canadian-owned oil. Thus, in view of this established pattern, it seems reasonable that we should seek to optimize the Canadian content of a northern pipeline, regardless of the ownership of the gas to be transported.
So we have precedents of joint energy undertakings by the two countries whereby the country that had the major part of the pipeline going through it received the majority of contracts for the labour and building of the pipeline. It would seem to me that the Canadian portion of the line would not contravene GATT or anger the United States unduly if we insisted upon maximizing Canadian content for it.
I am somewhat amazed at the way the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) leaps to the defence of the government on this issue, saying that we do not really need these guarantees in the legislation. I recall the comments of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). There is a steel plant in his area, and in the past he has called for guarantees. I recall, as well, the comments of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), who is worried that without guarantees the pipeline is a sell-out. I was struck not only by his wit but his good sense when he referred to the spurious argument put forward by the government, that the GATT prevented us from having guarantees in the legislation. As reported at page 2866 of Hansard he said:
The industry, trade and commerce report says that if we word it carefully we would have no problem with GATT. But this will not solve the project engineering services that are not affected by GATT. Japan, Germany and the United States don't care about GATT. The only ones who care about GATT are those in this "GATT government". The Canadian people have to get this GATT government so that it will not get them.

As I say, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Yukon and other members of the Conservative party who have castigated this government for not making policy, and for its disastrous handling of the unemployment situation all of a sudden embrace as the stone tablet from Mount Sinai, so to speak, the words of the Deputy Prime Minister as being good for all time. Yet they should not trust this minister and the government, but should want guarantees written into the legislation, rather than take their word that there will be some monitoring agency under the control of this government which, as we all know, will be dealing with so many matters after the fact, and we will not get the content we want.
I predict that without these amendments we will not get the 90 per cent content or the 100,000 man-hours of employment the government is so fond of talking about.
Motion No. 10 relates to the unfair trade practices part of the bill. When I think of the way this government has failed to defend Canadian industry, large or small, against unfair trade practices, I wonder how serious it is about making sure we are not underbid on contracts because of these unfair trade practices. That is why I moved my amendment to define what is meant by unfair trade practices so that the government cannot get off the hook when some of these problems occur. The amendment reads in part as follows:
"trade practices such as dumping, direct and indirect industrial subsidies, transportation subsidies and special tax incentives;"
The history of the steel industry in this country is quite clear. Countries such as Japan have been able to dump steel on the Canadian market, and Algoma Steel has proved this. We know, for example, that in order to get the contract for a Mexican gas pipeline, United States steel companies deliberately underbid by 20 per cent the whole cost of production. The object was to keep the mills in production rather than suffer temporary lay-offs. I think it is very important, therefore, that the government take these unfair trade practices into account.
I was appalled at the statement made in this House by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) when he said that we do not have to worry because we have our anti-dumping legislation which will suffice. I wonder how effective that legislation or any of our legislation is when put against the United States DISC program or the transportation subsidies given to Japanese steel, or the hidden tax subsidies given to West German and Italian steel companies. I do not know whether the government is monitoring all these factors. I do not know whether it will be able to show us that it will really look at the situation, should it occur. When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce stands in this House and gives a bland assurance that the anti-dumping legislation will suffice, I am appalled. We have it in Hansard that he let the cat out of the bag. He obviously was quoting from briefing notes, and quoted part of those notes he should not have.
I wish to refresh the memory of hon. members on this issue. It concerns the whole business of unfair competition. I refer to
April 3, 1978

page 3035 of Hansard. With regard to state subsidies and special tax concessions such as DISC, the minister stated, and I quote:
Action under the Anti-dumping Act could be taken in cases where exports into Canada are financed under more favourable terms than are available to the foreign manufacturer for its domestic sales. Under regulation (11 A) of the Anti-dumping regulations, credit and other financing terms can be taken into account in determining the normal value, export price, and, hence, the margins of dumping under the meaning of the act.
As I say, he should have stopped there, but he continued to read from his briefing notes, and this embarrassing statement came out:

Our steel industries can compete on a fair basis. We do not deny that. In fact, we support it. It is the unfair competition we are worried about. When talking about the steel industry, everyone seems to talk about the Ontario steel industry. There is another important plant, not as important now for the whole of the national economy as in the past, but terribly important for the people of Nova Scotia, especially those in eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton Island. There is another plant, not one that is integrated such as Stelco, Algoma or Dofasco, in Regina which is also very important. In order to put my concerns about the Sydney steel plant in perspective, I want to quote from a meeting of the Standing Committee on Regional Development held on Tuesday, March 21, 1978. I will skip over some parts and attempt not to distort the meaning of what was said, in an effort to get hon. members to realize that it is not only the Ontario steel industry involved here or whether the Ipsco plant in Regina will take part in these orders. In reality, world competitive conditions will decide in the ultimate analysis whether Canada will get a proper share of the pipe contracts.
I am not a member of this particular committee and, therefore, have not attended the committee meetings. However, I gather from what members of this party and other opposition members are saying, we are faced with a situation in which the determination of the steel content of the pipeline will be world competitive economic conditions.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), is basing a lot of fact on two points. The minister has said something very often. Many would probably be inclined to agree with him. I would question whether it is so. The last member of our party who spoke and most other members of our party feel the same about this. The two points emphasized by the Deputy Prime Minister are, first, that the Hamilton Stelco plant, with its pipe mill at Welland, does not have any worry. Because of its efficiency, it can compete against the Americans, Japanese, Italians and other Europeans. The type of pipe that will be used, the diameter and so on, will result in some spinoff to the Ipsco plant in Regina. Second, in addition, there will be a monitoring agency which will look at whether any unfair competitive practices will be followed by world competitors.
The Deputy Prime Minister and the government seem to believe that will guarantee us a fair share of the market, that it will mean 90 per cent Canadian content. 1 remind hon. members that, in the ultimate analysis, the Deputy Prime Minister is only saying that, in his opinion, the Canadian plants are capable of making this pipe and can compete because of their efficiency. That is the only guarantee we have.
You do not have to read too much Canadian economic history to realize that many types of barriers have been erected by other countries, especially the Japanese industry, which is a very different type of structured steel industry from our own.
Anyone who is familiar with the situation knows that the world steel industry is not an easy one to monitor. The previous speaker reminded us that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), referring to anti-dumping regulations, had mentioned that section 11 (a) had never really been tested. To my mind we are being totally unrealistic if we think only in terms of competition between Canada and the United States for these steel contracts in regard to the pipeline while completely ignoring the Italians, the rest of the European producers, and Japan.
The government appears to be depending upon world competitive conditions to maximize Canadian content. But consider the Japanese steel industry, for example. It is a private

Competing against the Japanese steel industry is not a matter of company against company; it is a matter of individual companies in Canada or the United States competing with the Japanese government.
The alliance between the Japanese government, industry, and labour has led to a unique situation. I do not know how many hon. members have read a fairly recent publication by Kenneth Galbraith entitled The New Industrial State. One of the reviewers of that book, another professor from Harvard University, said Mr. Galbraith, in his book, had given his readers new insights into the nature of multinational corporations and what are referred to as oligopolistic corporations, which means four or five industries which are capable of controlling output in such a way as to operate a good deal independent of the normal market restraints of supply and demand. As the previous speaker was making his point about the necessity of guarantees it occurred to me that the thesis of Mr. Galbraith's book was probably more applicable to the Japanese economy than to the economy of the United States. This is important because 1 believe the government itself has recently begun to realize that the economy is not working in the way the textbooks say it should. Things are not as they appeared when I taught Economics 100 and Economics 200.
Industry in Japan is so structured that it amounts to a corporate state in which private ownership is allowed to exist subject to a great deal of public control and regulation. The Japanese are not very interested in seeing that a particular steel firm makes a profit. They are concerned about whether that steel plan can produce efficiently enough to provide the steel necessary for construction, and especially for automobiles, at rates which will maintain Japanese exports in a strong position against world competition.
The point I am trying to make-and this is the third time I have repeated it-is this: in signing this guarantee, or in concluding this bilateral agreement with the United States, we acted under the assumption that the competition would largely be between Canadian and U.S. firms. The minister has contended that the provisions of GATT prevent us from insisting on guarantees. However, as the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) has so well argued, this is no ordinary agreement. It is a special agreement. Why is it a special agreement? It is special because we are giving the Americans a land bridge so that they may transport a product which they desperately need. Surely this is not the kind of multilateral agreement which is covered by GATT. I maintain it is a special type of bilateral agreement.
Not only are there non-tariff barriers surrounding the steel industry which are very difficult to fathom, but firms in western Europe, and, of course, in Japan, are supported by government to an extent far greater than is the case in North America. If the agreement had specified that the competition would be between Canada and the United States, we would today be in a different ball game altogether. Indeed, I would be inclined to agree with the thinking of the Deputy Prime Minister. But that is not the case. The companies which will be providing the gas obviously wish to keep their costs down so that they can make as much profit as possible. A number of the steel plants in the EEC countries, especially Italy, are in a position to supply the material which is needed. They have surplus capacity and they can produce the pipe. This being the case, I fear we may have to settle for 60 or 70 per cent instead of the 90 per cent the minister promised. Such a reduction would make an immense difference to the Sydney steel plant.
I know the Deputy Prime Minister is concerned in a general way that the Sydney steel plant should benefit from a spin-off effect in the form of orders for slabs and other materials which would be sent to Stelco, for example, which is expected to get a large share of the contract. But unless Canada gets 90 per cent of the work, there is little chance there will be any spin-off to the benefit of Cape Breton at a time the plant there desperately needs a shot in the arm.
When I asked Mr. McGee about this in the meeting of the regional economic committee, he told me it would take a year to a year and a half to complete studies on Sysco's renovation. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) is here, and he knows that what I am saying is true with regard to studies and action on the modernization of the Sydney steel plant, as reported by Mr. McGee, the Atlantic region administrator of DREE. Mr. Kent is the president of the Sydney Steel Corporation which, as most hon. members know, is under the provincial government of Nova Scotia and not under Devco where it should be, and when Mr. Kent appeared before the industry committee of the Nova Scotia government last week, he said that there would be a plan presented by the end of May. However, as I mentioned, just two weeks ago Mr. McGee told me that it would take a year to a year and a half before the studies would be completed and before it would be possible to take action. Mr. McGee went into detail, and I appreciated that very much. 1 am concerned about many things in this regard, but this is not the time to raise them all. I am concerned, however, about what will happen in the meantime, and one thing the Sydney plant vitally needs is a spin-off from the effects of this northern gas pipeline.
The Deputy Prime Minister is trained in economics, just as I have an academic economic background, and he knows that there is no way that there can be guarantees when the bidding is open to world competition. The Stelco pipe mill in Welland

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF OFFICE OF EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak against the motion moved by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) that the government should consider the advisability of establishing an office of education. I believe that at this time, when we are all concerned about fostering national unity, such a move would be regarded with deep distrust as an intrusion by the government of Canada into an area of provincial responsibility. Such a move would serve only to widen the gulf between the different levels of government rather than pulling us closer together as seems to be necessary today.
Historically, at the time of confederation the government of Canada played no role in education in Canadian society and the British North America Act placed the responsibility for education with provincial governments. The Government of Canada has been and is directly responsible for education in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, in the armed forces, in the penitentiary service, and for the education of Canada's native peoples.
Throughout our nation's history there have been many occasions on which the government of Canada has been called upon to play an active role in educational developments. For example, the government of Canada became involved in education in response to the educational demands of industrialization in the early 1900's, the demands of veterans returning from two world wars, and the enormous expansion of postsecondary enrolments in the 1960's. In each case, participation by the government of Canada was effected without usurping the authority of provincial governments and for the benefit of the country as a whole.
In 1966 Prime Minister Pearson clearly stated the position of the government of Canada with respect to education. He said:
Education is, under our constitution, a matter of provincial jurisdiction. The federal government does not dispute this or wish in any way to do so. At the
April 3, 1978

same time, education is obviously a matter of profound importance to the economic and social growth of the country as a whole... the federal government accepts primary responsibility for employment and economic activity generally in the country. We recognize that provincial governments share our concern in these matters and pursue these common aims in the conduct of their own affairs.
I believe that a review of the history of the involvement of the Government of Canada in education will demonstrate clearly that this involvement has occurred without usurping the constitutional rights of the provincial authorities.
Participation by the government of Canada in education dates back to 1876 when, in an effort to train more Canadians to serve as army officers, the Royal Military College was established at Kingston. Another early step was a 150,000 acre land endowment to the University of Manitoba in 1885, as provision for capital expenditures and establishment of a permanent source of revenue for the university. Although these early steps were of considerable significance, federal involvement was still quite limited in the latter part of the 19th century. Indeed, at that time education was considered to be a family responsibility and participation was largely determined by social status and religious belief. Public responsibility extended only to elementary schooling, and secondary schools, which were usually supported by religious organizations, were reserved to train future elites.
There was additional pressure on the Government of Canada in the early 1900's. This was linked specifically to the flow of young people from farms to cities, which began to jeopardize agricultural production, and to the shortage of skilled manpower in manufacturing industries. Following requests for action from business and labour, the Government of Canada appointed the Royal Commission on Industrial Training and Vocational Education in 1910. The work of the commission resulted in important legislation: the Agricultural Aid Act of 1912, and the Agricultural Instruction Act of 1913. The former supplied grants to provinces to develop agricultural education and techniques; the latter specifically gave assistance for training directly to the three existing veterinary colleges and, indirectly, by channelling funds through the provinces to agricultural colleges. This was the genesis of channelling federal aid for education through provincial governments.
In 1916, as a result of Canada's war involvement and a desire to improve research and development, the federal government formed the National Research Council. Initially, this was an effort to co-ordinate government research programs. During World War II, the National Research Council played a vital role in co-ordinating and conducting scientific research. The Council now has an extensive program of grants and fellowships.
When the federal government established the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in 1918, provision was made for a division to be concerned with education statistics. The education division published its first statistical report in 1921, and it has expanded its services and publications considerably since then.
Office of Education
The economic depression of the 1930's served to identify a major problem within the secondary school system. On school leaving, many students found that they had few occupational skills with which to enter the labour market. In an attempt to alleviate this problem, the federal government introduced a new program for technical education in 1937 with the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act. This act, directed towards maintaining the morale and increasing the employability of young people, was negotiated in agreement with the provinces, on a cost-sharing basis, through the establishment of various occupational training projects. Eligibility was limited to those between the ages of 18 and 30. Emphasizing vocational and technical skill, this Act initially provided funds of about $2.5 million during its two years, but corrected only to a limited degree the inadequacies of technical and vocational education.
A Royal Commission on Dominion-Provincial Relations, known as the Rowell-Sirois Commission, was appointed in 1937 to make an assessment of the economic and financial basis of confederation; the distribution of federal and provincial powers; and federal-provincial financial relations. While its mandate did not extend to education, the commission felt that equality of educational opportunity did come within its domain. According to the commission, the concept "education" had changed and expanded to include new dimensions since the time of the BN A Act.
In view of this, the commission recommended that "the federal government should have full power to provide employment aid for those recognized as employable-which would make the training of unemployed youth a matter of even greater federal concern than at present." The commission assumed that the provinces would provide a system of courses to those Canadians requiring further training.
While the commission stated that a free hand in education was vital to provincial autonomy, it identified certain problems arising in this context. Representations were made to the commission concerning "the existence in several provinces of a sense of grievance which may well contribute to national disunity as well as to lack of harmony within the province concerned." Although the commission lamented the disparity in educational opportunity throughout the country, it made no relevant recommendations. Solutions rested on financial proposals which would place the provinces in a position to meet their responsibilities for education, if they chose to do so.
The commission also suggested that a council, analogous to the National Research Council, could be established to support research work in the social sciences in Canadian universities and elsewhere. The commission suggested, furthermore, that it might be appropriate for the federal government to establish a national library.
Growing Canadian cultural awareness and concern for a Canadian identity prompted the federal government to appoint in 1949 the Royal Commission on National Development in the Arts, Letters and Sciences. problems: scarcity of financial aid to the arts and humanities; the financial condition of universities; and orientation toward a small educated elite. As the commission noted, the number of veterans enrolling as students was quickly diminishing and, as a result, the federal aid that came with them was eroding. The commission believed that action was urgently required in this sector and that it was the duty of the federal government to assist in some way.
In view of the fact that the Canadian constitution did not forbid financial assistance to a citizen in order to help him to carry on studies in his chosen field, the commission did not feel that it would be improper to recommend federal aid in the form of contributions to individuals. A further recommendation was the continuation of federal support for the program of the National Research Council. As for disciplines outside of the boundaries of natural science, the commission recommended the establishment of what is today the Canada Council.
Perhaps I should stop at that point because we have certainly run into problems as a result of the establishment of this council. I would certainly recommend that the government look at the present Canada Council appointments and especially at whether parliament should in some way be involved with the appointment of people to the Canada Council instead of the present system whereby they are appointed under the direction of the Secretary of State.
Many of us are aware that some of the publications which have been subsidized by the Council-and I refer particularly to the Blue Ointment Press in Vancouver-are a degradation to the printed word in Canada. At a time when this parliament is examining the question of pornography and legislation to curb it, it seems very strange that pornographic materials should be published under the auspices of the Canada Council. I hope members on both sides will look very seriously at a body appointed by the federal government to determine whether funds should be appropriated to assist artists, novelists and poets which degrades itself by publishing pornographic materials. I think the House should look at this question, whether in a committee or whether when brought up on estimates.
I think there should be some regulation governing the Canada Council whereby members of this House would have the right to assist in appointments. In an attempt to be fair and impartial, so that decisions are not made by political bodies as to what is art and what is not and as to what should be funded in the cultural area, what has happened is that in appointing people who have a knowledge of the arts something has gone wrong, and material which should not be published is being published under the auspices of the Canada Council. I say that more in sorrow than in anger because I feel that the Canada Council has an important role to play in Canadian culture. However, if publications such as the one I mentioned by the Blue Ointment Press of Vancouver are published as a result of government funding, I suggest that a thorough examination should be made so that Canadian culture rather than Canadian pornography is advanced.

In view of the fact that the Canadian constitution does not forbid financial assistance to citizens, I wonder if I may raise another point which I think should be considered, since very seldom do we have the opportunity to discuss education in the House of Commons. It appears from what has occurred in the last several years that our educational system is not providing the skills which are needed in the work force. One of the highest rates of unemployment in Canada can be found among students.
I think we are dealing with an antiquated system. Our society needs more skilled people every year, but our students, while being educated, are not acquiring the skills required by the labour market. Perhaps even more importantly, they are coming out of high school without any definition as to what their role in society might be. High school graduates are going from job to job because they have not considered future occupations, and they are not being advised what opportunities there are or what path they should be taking. As time goes on I think it will become more and more important that there be guidance at both the provincial and federal levels. At a time when our school enrolments are decreasing our universities are attracting more and more students. I certainly do not believe that the Government of Canada has any right to step in and say to a person that he cannot make use of certain facilities because there is no forseeable need for certain skills; but this information should at least be made available.
Surely students should be counselled before they enter faculties of education or faculties of general arts. They should be told that their skills may not be needed, so that if they proceed they will at least know that they may have problems finding jobs upon graduation. For a number of years students have not been counselled as to what jobs might be available in the future or made aware that some job opportunities may diminish as time goes on because of a variety of factors. The birth rate has decreased over the last 15 years or so, and in the future fewer schools and fewer teachers will be required.
A great deal of work can be done, not necessarily through an educational council, but through working with the provinces. There have been various conferences in the last month or two at which federal and provincial governments have discussed matters of common concern. Earlier in the pipeline debate I said that there will be a crucial shortage of trained personnel when pipeline construction begins. At the present time we do not have enough welders and mechanics. We know that the pipeline will be coming on stream. Therefore, provincial and federal governments should be making arrangements. They should not wait until construction begins; these arrangements should be made several years in advance. That to me seems elementary. However, are we making those arrangements now? Is the federal government, in conjunction with the provinces, doing that?
I honestly believe that we do not need another bureaucracy. We need departments-for example, the Department of Employment and Immigration-which use common sense. Federal and provincial departments together should determine what the needs will be in the foreseeable future and work
April 3, 1978
together. We need heavy duty mechanics. There is not one logging camp or mine in British Columbia which is not advertising for heavy duty mechanics. There are many people who wish to work, but I suggest there are not enough skilled people; one does not have to be the most gifted parliamentarian to understand that. On an almost daily basis business people come to me telling me that they cannot get Canadian labour and asking me if they can hire labour from outside Canada. What have we been doing with our education system for the last ten years? Why do we not know what our requirements are in the field of specialized skills? We are going to require more people with special skills when pipeline construction begins.
