speechtext:
As soon as I start giving an explanation as to where I was, the very same minister who asked for that explanation now interrupts by saying "Order".
In dealing with Bill C-18, it is critical for the House to realize how inept the federal government has been with respect to the handling of our economy, and in particular, the handling of the inflation situation in this country. The fact is the government has failed to give a proper explanation to the

4086

April 3, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
House, or certainly to a committee of the House, as to why its so-called anti-inflation program has failed so miserably.
We must bear in mind that we were told by the government this year that our inflation level would be down to 4 per cent by about October. Incidentally, the Minister of Finance keeps changing his story. Initially we were told in committee by the Minister of Finance that the inflation level in Canada would be 6 per cent during 1978. Realizing how devious this minister can be and how he twists his terms, we zeroed in specifically at committee and said: "Mr. Minister, would you explain? What do you mean by 6 per cent? Do you mean come June, 12 months over June 1977, it will be 6 per cent? Is it the average 1978 inflation level over the average 1977?" He said: "No doubt about that; I am talking average 1978 over average 1977". Within two weeks the minister reversed himself and said that he meant a 6 per cent inflation level in December this year compared to December 1977. That is an entirely different picture. The present Minister of Finance is about the only Canadian who believes today, if he in turn believes, that we are going to reach even a 6 per cent inflation level by December 1978.
The reason I refer to the sorry progress of this government with respect to Bill C-18, both in the House and in committee, is that when the government returned to the House and asked for this amending legislation to be passed in order to patch up some of the deficiencies in the initial anti-inflation program, I would have thought any responsible minister of finance would have said: "I feel you in the House should be given a full accounting of how the program has worked, a blow by blow description of how we have failed and where we have been successful in the anti-inflation program". I would have expected the minister to outline where the fiscal restraint, which was promised in October 1975, was felt in the economy. None of us can find the spending restraint which they claimed in October 1975 was going to be followed. I expected the Minister of Finance to explain why the monetary growth has been so aggressive since October 1975, yet we were told that they were going to be more restrained in their monetary growth at that time. Also, the Minister of Finance should have indicated where the promised deregulation took place since October 1975. In fact, more government regulation, not less, has been put on Canadian industry and the Canadian public since then.
I make these points to outline how the government has not given a proper accounting in the House regarding its antiinflation program. Most importantly, the activities of the Anti-Inflation Board and the entire effect of the so-called anti-inflation program has been glossed over by the government. For example, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) attempted to get away with certain misstatements today during question period, when he indicated that somehow or other our economy was doing tremendously well. I do not know why he singled out Japan, but he indicated that, other than Japan, Canada is doing better than anyone else. That is an untruth which he put forward in the House and generally to the Canadian public.

Let me be specific on this important subject. In the February 1978 Bank of Canada Review there is a very interesting analysis of what the bank calls the international economic and financial developments in 1977. This report was prepared by the international department of the bank, under the direction of Mr. John White. At page 10, table II, it is made quite clear that Canada's record, as far as inflation is concerned, has been a disaster in spite of the controls program which we are now being asked to patch up, in the sense of relieving some of the deficiencies existent in the program from day one.
Every hon. member should read the entire Bank of Canada article, and in particular, what is said with respect to Bill C-18 concerning consumer prices. In the 12 month period of December 1976 to December 1977, the inflation level shown for Canada is 9.5 per cent. Of course, that is the rate put out by Statistics Canada on that date. The performances of seven major industrialized nations of the world have been reviewed. Included in the United States, Japan, Germany, France, United Kingdom, Italy and Canada. Inflation in those countries for that one year period ending last December reached a high of 7.2 per cent. So we have the startling revelation by the statistical department of the Bank of Canada, which is confirmed nothwithstanding the anti-inflation program introduced by the government in October 1975, that we have had higher inflation than other countries during the same period. In fact, our inflation was 2.3 per cent higher. When one reviews the figures of the Bank of Canada, perhaps the most serious observation to make is that our main trading partner has consistently had a better inflation record without controls than we have had with controls.
It is unforgiveable for the Minister of Finance to sit in the House tonight and remain mum about these facts when we are reviewing a bill designed to amend the legislation about which when it was brought in the government was saying it would perform such magic with inflation. This minister owes an explanation on behalf of his former minister of finance, and certainly on behalf of his emperor, sometimes called the Prime Minister of this country, as to why this country's record has unfortunately been so much worse than the economic records of other countries.
Let me go back to what I think is a most serious revelation, and that is the comparison of Canada's inflation level at various time periods, reviewed in the "Bank of Canada Review", with the inflation level for the same time periods of the United States, our main trading partner. For example, we find that in the 12 months ended December, 1975 the U.S. inflation level was 7 per cent while our inflation level was 9.5 per cent. For the 12 months ended June, 1976 the United States brought its inflation level down to 5.9 per cent, and I emphasize that this was without controls, whereas Canada's inflation level was still 7.8 per cent. For the 12 months ended December, 1976 the United States inflation level was down to 4.8 per cent-below 5 per cent-yet the Canadian rate was 5.8 per cent, still above the U.S. level. By the 12 months ended in
April 3, 1978

June, 1977 the U.S. inflation rate was 6.8 per cent compared to the Canadian rate of 7.8 per cent.
In short, for every period to which I have referred there has been a worse Canadian inflation rate than that of the United States. In the last 12 months period ending in December the Canadian inflation rate was worse than the rate of any of the seven major industrialized nations, and certainly worse than the inflation rate of our main trading partner, the United States. For the 12 months period ended December last year the United States inflation rate was 6.8 per cent compared to an unbelievable Canadian rate of 9.5 per cent. This is the background for the debate we are entering into tonight, and these are the facts we must consider when deciding whether this government should receive support for Bill C-18, to amend the anti-inflation legislation.
As we know, the bank rate has been increased again tonight. This government has sought and obtained an additional $1 billion stand-by credit from our Canadian chartered banks. In all likelihood a revelation will be made tomorrow morning concerning the outflow of funds from our foreign exchange which will truly startle the international market once again. As I said today during the question period, it has been estimated there probably was an outflow of $500 million during March. My advisers quite frankly tell me it was much more; I was trying to low-ball the facts today. In fact, we believe this outflow could have been as much as $700 million during the month of March. In any event, we are going to know these figures in the morning.
In asking for an additional $1 billion to shore up the Canadian dollar, this government is clearly anticipating the anxiety to be felt tomorrow not only by Canadians but by the international market regarding our falling dollar and the state of our foreign exchange fund.
Is it surprising that we have this dilemma of high unemployment, high inflation and a current account deficit four times that of the average deficit of any major industrialized nation in the world? Is it surprising when we realize that since last December there has been thrust upon us a Minister of Finance who has turned out to be only a part-time minister? This is a position that requires the full-time attention of our best available person; but unfortunately we do not have such a man in our present Minister of Finance.
Having regard to the plight of our dollar, how often have we been told that somehow or other the fact that our dollar has depreciated or is falling in value has resulted suddenly in more attractive exports in international trade? We have been told that somehow or other we should have had a discounted dollar long ago. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) has told us that in his view an 89 cent dollar is a good thing for Canada.
I point out these facts because I believe this government has no idea of the effect of a cheap dollar on the inflation rate in this country. It is interesting to note that at page 10 of the "Bank of Canada Review", to which I have already referred, Mr. White comments concerning the falling dollar situation in
Anti-Inflation Act
Italy and the United Kingdom that occurred a few years ago. He states;
In Italy and the United Kingdom where depreciation of their currencies have added to inflationary pressures the relative stability of both the lire and the pound this past year contributed to slower rates of price increases.
What Mr. White is confirming in that article is that a falling dollar means more inflation in the country whose currency is falling. It is as simple as that. Unfortunately our dollar has been falling because this government has been less than candid and less than clear as to the level at which it deems the Canadian dollar should be trading. This government's lack of knowledge about how to handle this type of problem has resulted in an undermining of world confidence as far as international money markets are concerned. This has created the impression that this government would somehow or other welcome an even lower level for our dollar. This is virtually a bottomless pit, and it apparently does not matter how far the dollar drops.
During one of the briefing sessions for Canadian businessmen by the Department of Finance the businessmen were floored when an official, asked if he would worry should our dollar drop to 80 cents, said that a floating dollar is a floating dollar, and if it goes to 80 cents, that is where it goes. That is not how international money markets operate. Other countries expect governments to have confidence in their ability to handle the economic affairs of their countries and they expect those governments to be able to indicate whether their currency is at a fair level in a specific range.
What this goverment has been doing is pretending on the one hand that it has not interfered with the behaviour of our dollar on international markets, while on the other hand it has been using hundreds of millions of dollars from our United States foreign exchange reserves to defend the dollar that it claims it would like to see float even lower. The sad result is that we now have the worst of all worlds. This is the result of this government's hard-nosed measures and tendencies to have the dollar dribble down and down in value, while at the same time allowing our reserves to be dissipated. Perhaps when the figures are revealed tomorrow we will find we have lost $1.5 billion of our reserves since January 1, while at the same time we have a dollar valued obviously much below the point to which the government felt it should fall.
Our dollar would not be trading at today's level if we had a government which inspired international confidence. This government can fool many Liberals in this country, as it likes to do; it can fool many Canadian voters, as it wants to do; but it will not fool for any prolonged period of time, if at all, those hardnosed international financiers of this world. This government has now faced up to the stark reality of having to deal with international bankers who do not want rhetoric or charisma, but rather, hard, cold facts about how our economy, which is obviously out of whack, is to be righted.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker, and it is pertinent when we are dealing with Bill C-18 to bear them in mind because I

April 3, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
do not feel that this government even now has learned the lesson that their spending programs, previously and currently, their monetary increases, and that type of policy bring inflation which, in turn, undermines international confidence. This means that our currency will be put at a lower price level in relation to the other harder currencies; but perhaps they would like to see that.
When I say this I think of one piece of misrepresentation that we must put on the record and make sure there is no doubt, so far as Canadians are concerned, as to what it is all about. This government likes to fool various people. They went into New York and they tried in their way to fudge the issue concerning our economic picture for 1979. We have never been able to get a firm statement from this government as to what their revenue and expenditure position will be in the coming year. They have tried to fudge the issue.
When this government went to New York with a preliminary prospectus issued on March 8, 1978, they tried to get by with simply showing the fiscal 1978 figures for Canada and making no disclosure as to what the deficit might be for 1979. Frankly-and you will recall some of the questioning in this House, Mr. Speaker-this surprised us because we were told by certain investment officials with the American government: "There is no way that we were going to tolerate the Canadian government not making full, true and plain disclosure before $750 million was loaned to them" which is what the government was seeking effective April 1, 1978. They said: "Tell us what will be your cash deficit where 1979 is concerned; come clean." Let there be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that is why this little Minister of Finance crept into this House on March 16 and gave a statement as to what in fact the deficit would be as far as cash needs for 1979 are concerned.
We now find that on March 22 the March 8 preliminary prospectus filed in Washington was changed to give a more complete disclosure as to the plight we are actually facing in Canada. There is a new footnote put into that prospectus and it very interestingly says this:
In a statement by the Minister of Finance on March 16, 1978, it was indicated that financial requirements for Fiscal 1978 are now expected to total $8,800 million-
This is up decidedly from what they tried to get by with showing in Washington and New York. The footnote goes on to state:
-and are anticipated to be about $11,000 million for fiscal 1979.
I think it is a tragedy that we have a government, led by the emperor, who is now so indifferent to knowledge in Canada. And to our right to have the facts, that he has no compunction through his Minister of Finance about refusing to give out facts until he is brought to his knees in Washington and New York, and only when his bankers said: "Unless you tell us those facts you are not going to get your money".
We are now dealing with a new problem as far as foreign financing is concerned, and this was revealed earlier today. The long end of the American issue that was placed in New York is now selling at a discount of $1.75. It was brought out at par, Mr. Speaker, and it is now trading at $88.25; and if

you want to undermine the confidence of international investors still further, pull that kind of trick on them. Sell them an issue effective on April 1, tell them it is properly priced, that you think there is an equitable rate structure put on your issue, and then on Monday, April 3 have them live with a $1.75 discount on the issue that you have sold them. Try selling another issue, Mr. Speaker, as you need further funds down the road, and you will receive a very chilly reception.
I mention this because of the news today. The increased bank rate, the increase in our line of credit with our own Canadian chartered banks, means the government is going to have to go back to the international trough once again and say: "Please give us another bail-out". What I am suggesting is that, because of the way the present issue has been handled, they are going to get a pretty chilly reception. Let there be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, when I say that the issue fell to $1.75 discount from its issue price, the long end of it; that put it into perspective. It now means that in the eye of international investors, Canada's credit rating is lower than that of most of the major U.S. corporation credits.
Most of the large finance companies in the United States are now being given money at a cheaper yield than Canada is able to borrow in that international market. It is very humiliating for a nation with the resources and talented people we have in Canada to have to live with a situation where our national credit is put on a basis junior or more speculative than the credit of certain corporations, including finance companies, in the United States. Those are the facts.
In dealing with Bill C-18, Mr. Speaker, we have got to bite the bullet. The reason our dollar has gotten into its present plight and that we are on bended knee in New York and Washington asking for more and more foreign borrowing is because the inflation program of this government did not work. As I said at the beginning, we have higher inflation than the combined inflation levels of seven industrialized nations of the world. Every year that the program has been in effect our inflation level has been running higher than the inflation level in the United States, and that to international investors means that our dollar has to go down in relation to the American dollar. And down it went.
The government, in an attempt to make a bad thing look good, has said the discounted dollar is the best thing that was ever invented and that somehow or other it is going to spur the economy. I have already read into the record John White's comment as to what happened with a depreciated dollar in Italy and the United Kingdom. The fact is that a discounted dollar that is lower as far as its relationship, for example, to the American dollar is concerned, is only a good thing if you take advantage of the competitive position it artificially gives. A depreciated dollar is only good if you can get a handle on your own inflation to ensure that the depreciation that you are now trying to utilize will remain and keep you competitive with your international competitors. The United Kingdom tried lowering the value of their pound, and we find today that if their oil revenue is taken out they are still running a substantial current account deficit with the rest of the world,
April 3, 1978

in spite of their so-called depreciations or devaluations. On the other hand, the Germans have never had a devaluation or a depreciation. They have had nothing but a surplus with the rest of the world.
Those are the hard facts. We will not gain permanently by simply depreciating our dollar. In fact, it becomes a repetitive thing-the more you depreciate the more your inflation goes up; the more inflation goes up the more you have got to depreciate still further. There is no doubt the government would rather see our dollar higher, and every protestation that they make that somehow the dollar is a good thing at 87 cents is simply trying to let on that a bad thing is a good thing. Elowever, it will not be bought internationally. If it was otherwise, surely we could ask the government why they encouraged the dollar to go to $ 1.03 premium at one time; why did they go to our corporations and municipalities and our provinces and ask them to go into foreign lands to borrow money? Why did they drop the withholding tax to facilitate borrowing that money in order to keep up the Canadian dollar if at the same time they thought it was a bad thing to have a high Canadian dollar? They cannot have it both ways. If they now say it is a good thing to have an 87-cent dollar, that must mean it was a bad thing when the dollar was at $1.00 or $1.03. On the other hand, if it is good to have an 87-cent dollar, why is it not even better to have a 77-cent dollar or a 50-cent dollar? How is it that the magic level that the so-called floating dollar reaches is always the ideal level, according to this government? I think we know the answer, Mr. Speaker. The government is in a tizzy. It is panicking. Its political expediency does not jell with economic reality. Today we have perhaps the greatest indication of how political expediency rules as far as this government is concerned.
In spite of the fact that it has been generally felt that we needed new budgetary measures six months ago, or possibly twelve months ago, the government consistently said they were not needed and that the economy was doing better than most economists said, that inflation was better than most economists said, and that real growth was better. In March, 1977, the previous minister of finance-now gone like so many other ministers-said that unemployment would be less toward the end of 1977 because of the imaginative provisions he brought in. Yet we now have the highest unemployment of any industrialized nation in the world.
This is the record of this government, Mr. Speaker. It asks us virtually to rubber stamp this bill, to pass this act for the anti-inflation program. I think it behooves us to ask why this part-time Minister of Finance is not willing to stand up in this House and give a full explanation of the failings of the anti-inflation program.
On that score, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should be more specific about why I feel he is a part-time minister. We have never had a Minister of Finance so reluctant to come before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. We cannot get him there.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
We hoped to receive information in return. There were certain amendments we proposed to make to the bill and we wanted to get it out of second reading and into committee for study. We got it into committee and there was,
I suppose the term is "leaked" to us, certain draft legislation concerning the setting up of an inflation monitoring agency and also another bill called the Financial and Compensation Data Returns Act.
We were left with the impression, from the responses of the minister in committee, that we had caught the government slightly off guard-that they had tried to slip Bill C-18 through, hoping the legislation would remain dormant, that nobody would question it and that they subsequently intended to bring in both these bills for which we had the drafts.
When we brought this matter up, the minister's response was rather odd. First of all, he said he knew nothing about the legislation and did not know what I was talking about. It was pointed out that the draft legislation had his name on the first page. It said that "minister" means "minister of finance". Clearly if somebody had been drafting legislation that the minister knew nothing about it was a most curious thing, and it makes one wonder what the government is up to. We pressed the point and there was a kind of admission that maybe at some lower echelon someone might have been toying with draft bills. In any event, the minister wanted no part of it.
In order to facilitate the questioning of the minister- because up to that point he had refused to acknowledge there was such draft legislation-I offered him the draft, but he said he did not want to touch it. It was untouchable, Mr. Speaker. I can only presume that if any member of the House was minister of finance and someone came to committee with a draft bill that said he was the minister referred to in the bill, he would be curious to find out what was going on. This minister, however, said he did not want to touch it. We pressed him and the answer was to the effect that really it did not have much to do with Bill C-18. In fact it had everything to do with Bill C-18 because it is on the question of what happens after the anti-inflation program ends. The impression was left that this does not have too much to do with Bill C-18, that the Prime Minister had asked the Economic Council of Canada to do the monitoring but certainly they did not want any provisions like those referred to in the draft legislation.
It was a stand off, Mr. Speaker. In effect, we said if the government want us to pass Bill C-18, they had better come clean and tell us what they have in mind for a monitoring

April 3, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
agency and this so-called returns act, which had provisions such that people could go to jail for years if they almost inadvertently failed to sent in a requested report. The result- and I do not disagree-was that the chairman suggested we adjourn the committee until it was clear what the Economic Council was going to do. If it is not going to get into monitoring, clearly some provision will have to be made for monitoring, and this legislation, or something similar, will have to be brought in. I emphasize that the aura that the minister tried to put around it was that there was nothing to the draft legislation I referred to; that it was almost a figment of someone's imagination and he did not contemplate bringing in legislation immediately.
That leads me to the delay, Mr. Speaker. It was decided to postpone future meetings because in fairness it was felt the minister should be given the opportunity to get his house in order. It was not clear whether he was going to go the Economic Council route, or the route of some legislation along the lines of that I referred to.
The plot thickens, Mr. Speaker. As you know, the illustrious emperor, the Prime Minister, sent a letter to Dr. Ostry of the Economic Council of Canada dated March 15 and signed by his own hand. It set out very, very interesting things that he requested the Economic Council to do.
As a preliminary matter, perhaps I should make it clear that in effect what has now followed is that we have an Anti-Inflation Board carrying on with respect to the bulk of Canadian companies and workers till December 31, 1978; but as of April 14 we have Dr. Ostry and her posse coming into the picture to scrutinize what is going on in the nation with respect to inflation. Specifically, it refers to her checking out and "analyzing price and cost developments in the national economy". Those are the emperor's actual words.
I mention this because it is absolutely hypocritical of this government to pretend to the Canadian public that they are doing all these monitoring procedures, that they are desperately trying to identify who is the villain as far as prices are concerned, who the villain is on the labour side, whether the small shopkeeper or whoever, without accepting the responsibility for inflation. They do not have to go 100 yards from where they stand to find out where inflation is created in this country. It is literally created on the south side of Wellington Street by the printing of an excess amount of money in reference to the real growth of the economy. Any economist will acknowledge that.
This government is allowing the printing presses to be run through the Bank of Canada facility. It allowed 12 per cent more money to be created in Canada last year than the year before, in spite of the fact we only had 6.2 per cent real growth. I said our inflation was 9.5 per cent. Is it any mystery? Add up those figures and you will see why we have the inflation to which I am referring.
Is it not hypocritical for a government to pretend, presumably for political reasons, that they are trying earnestly to do

something about inflation? They are now setting up a two-tier level of monitoring and supervision of inflation when they have been goosing the economy through the printing of excess money. Those are the hard facts.
When dealing with the role of the Economic Council, I want to draw to the attention of hon. members a very interesting fact. The Minister of Finance said that the draft legislation that I referred to had no meaning, or somehow or other was virtually a figment of somebody's imagination. However, when we review the letter from the Prime Minister to Dr. Ostry of March 15, we find that he sets out from A to F the various jobs he would like the Economic Council to do. Save for a realignment of paragraphs and a few changes of words, we find what he has asked Dr. Ostry to do is almost word for word what was in the draft legislation bearing the name of the Minister of Finance, which he told us in committee he knew nothing about. If we are to believe the Minister of Finance, something is really amiss in the Department of Finance and throughout the entire government. Presumably somebody is on the loose drafting legislation and is sufficiently in the know that his terminology is able to leap into the Prime Minister's letter to Dr. Ostry and be adopted by no less than the Prime Minister as the terms of reference for the Economic Council of Canada to follow in carrying out their monitoring procedures.
When I started to bring this out in committee, I was rather startled to find that the well-primed chairman of that committee was quick to say that it had no relevance to Bill C-18, in spite of the fact we delayed any further meetings of the committee until we could understand what the role of the Economic Council of Canada would be. We were told it would have no relevance. When we persisted, the Minister of Finance quickly refused to answer any questions. He said that what the Prime Minister said in the letter was not his business, that he would answer anything concerning Bill C-18 but not get into the role of the Economic Council in relation to monitoring or what-have-you.
The reason this is important is that if hon. members read the October 20, 1975 statement of this government, the fourth prong or wheel of their anti-inflation program was a deregulation of the Canadian economy. They said that was going to relieve-and I believe it would have-the present constriction within the economy that is contributing to inflation.
The program really had four wheels. It had de-regulation for the first wheel, fiscal restraint for the second wheel, monetary restraint for the third wheel and the AIB activities to which this bill is addressed for the fourth. Where it is relevant to concern ourselves with the Economic Council, in spite of the fact that the other three wheels have not worked worth a darn, namely fiscal restraint, monetary restraint and de-regulation, we find that the government is now proposing through its approach to the Economic Council of Canada a continuation of the AIB to have still further regulation and supervision of our industry beyond anything that was ever conceived.
It is important to bear in mind that the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board gave us the following estimates of the
April 3, 1978

percentage of companies, professional firms and employees who would be released from controls by various dates. Bear in mind the government has represented that their de-phasing or de-control period will begin on April 14 of this year. It is important that we remember what they mean by that.
The chairman of the AIB made clear that by May 1, 1978, only 9 per cent of the employees in Canada, 9 per cent of the companies and 4 per cent of the professionals will be free from the AIB activities. By June 1,13 per cent of the employees, 10 per cent of the companies and 8 per cent of the professionals will be free. By October 1, 62 per cent of the employees, 78 per cent of the companies and 77 per cent of the professional people will still be bound by the anti-inflation program. On December 1, 53 per cent of Canadian employees, 68 per cent of the companies and 75 per cent of our professionals will still be bound by the program. Let us get that into perspective. Until December 1 this year, the majority of the employees, over two thirds of the companies and three quarters of our professional people will still be bound by the Anti-Inflation Board rulings and the whole program, notwithstanding the de-phasing that begins on April 14.
I put those figures on record because there has been too much talk that somehow we are suddenly going to go out of controls. In truth, that is not right. We are not out of controls until very late this year. In fact, the chairman of the AIB made it clear that they do not see us being completely clear of the AIB for at least a year after December 31, 1978.
We are in the position tonight of having to face the fact that the government has represented that de-controls begin on April 14, when in all likelihood de-controls in the form they anticipate will not be effective until well into December of this year for the bulk of our businesses, employees and professional people. That is the main point I want to make on this subject.
Notwithstanding that degree of control, we find that the Prime Minister, in the letter to which I referred, has asked the Economic Council of Canada to do an overview of everything that has been happening. Not only is it an overview, but on page three of his letter the Prime Minister states:
Because of the potential importance of an individual price or cost increase and the need for information which is not publicly available, however, it may be considered by the Council or-
I would stress the word "or".
-the government that a special inquiry into a particular case is warranted. It is recognized that the carrying on of such special inquiries into individual price or cost increases under the powers of the Inquiries Act may be needed from time to time, but that such special inquiries would not be appropriately carried out by the Council itself. Such special inquiries would, however, be facilitated by the assistance provided from the Council's ongoing analyses and staff support.
On this basis and pursuant to Part 10 of the Economic Council of Canada Act, I therefore request that the Council undertake a specific responsibility for analyzing price and cost developments in the national economy. More particularly under this reference, the Council would exercise the following duties, subject to the description and limitations set out above:
He then lists the terms of reference he would like the Economic Council to follow. They are essentially the terms of reference anticipated in the government's draft inflation moni-
Anti-Inflation Act
toring agency act to be carried out by that agency should the act ever be passed.
Not only do we find these two levels, but the Prime Minister goes on to say he feels the Council should review the situation for two years. These are his words addressed to Dr. Ostry:
You should discuss with the Treasury Board the provision of the additional resources which the Council will require in order to carry out these additional duties.
Nobody knows the number of additional staff the Economic Council feels it should have in order to carry out this new monitoring function. It has been estimated that 100 additional civil servants will be needed. News accounts from various sources are now making it clear that in any event there will be no abandonment of the 700 employees who presently work for the AIB. Thus we may end up with 700 employees from the AIB "doing their thing", plus another 100 people working for the Economic Council, all hoping to get a handle on inflation in Canada.
Referring to the employees of the AIB, an article in the April 1 edition of the Financial Post states:
There are several hundred who are full-time civil servants and these people have been guaranteed new government jobs with no cut in pay.
Think of the scenario. We have the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) credibly arguing that the time has come to cut down the public service, not by firing people but through the ordinary process of attrition; and at the same time the government, so we are assured in this article, has guaranteed that these employees will not lose their government jobs or suffer any reduction in pay. Yet this is a perfect example of an area in which they could cut down costs. The article in the Financial Post went on to say:
The AIB's middle managers have been preparing one-page resumes on all of these people. The resumes are being sent to all government departments to be used in filling job vacancies-when the AIB is ready to let them go.
Most of these workers will be released toward the end of the year. Blackwell-
That is the name of an official quoted earlier in the article.
-concedes there is a danger the job market could be temporarily flooded but he predicts the huge Ottawa bureaucracy will absorb the workers fairly smoothly.
Is it not almost laughable to find a government which pretends it is a government of restraint giving ironclad guarantees that none of these employees will lose their jobs or suffer pay cuts?
I am giving this background because I think we must accept the fact that, should the party opposite ever be returned with a majority to this House, the controls program will not end. What they intend to do, through this devious approach, is to reignite the entire controls system at the earliest opportunity and inflict it, perhaps for an indefinite period, upon the Canadian public. 1 do not think there is any doubt about it. The Prime Minister believes in controls. He has lost faith in our system. He no longer believes in the economy of the marketplace. He does not believe that the system which has brought prosperity to this nation can build an ever greater nation on the basis of free enterprise. Somehow he has accepted the line of the socialists, the supporters of the NDP, that an even greater degree of state intervention and control is needed

April 3, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
in order to secure increased prosperity. He does not realize that exactly the reverse is the case, and that if we wish to turn the economy around what we need is a renewed vigour on the part of the private enterprise system as opposed to an extension of government controls.
We are dealing tonight with a big subject. Bill C-18 is a measure which contains many clauses and it is important we should deal with some of its inconsistencies and draw attention to amendments which ought to have been considered before the legislation left the finance committee. Hon. members who took part in the meetings of the finance committee on the bill will, I am sure, agree with me that it was passed only under the guillotine. The more the Minister of Finance refused to answer questions concerning the anti-inflation program the more the Liberal members on the committee insisted that the measure should be passed at once. Using the brutal majority they exercise in every committee of the House they insisted that the bill be passed without the benefit of further evidence from the part-time Minister of Finance or of amendments which we on this side thought were needed.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to be specific. I will begin by drawing attention to clauses 1 and 8. Clause 8, as undoubtedly Your Honour knows, makes the application of clause 1 retroactive to December 16, 1975, which is the date of the order in council establishing the regulations of the AntiInflation Act itself. Clause 1 enlarges the coverage of the present guidelines to include businesses in trucking, shipping, longshoring and grain handling sectors which bargain collectively. The amendment in C-18 ensures that profit guidelines will apply to companies which as a wage negotiating group form a unit large enough to merit control. The Anti-Inflation Act is constructed in such a way that wage-earners come under controls when the employing company comes under control. The amendment would also enlarge the coverage of wage controls.
Some additional construction companies are also brought under the controls by use of the same method applied to transportation industries. The companies and unions identified in clause 1 were brought under controls on April 22, 1976 by Order in Council P.C. 1976-910: SOR/76-273. The order came into effect on April 15, 1976 and was issued under the authority of section 3(2)(a)(v) of the Anti-Inflation Act. Before that section could be used it was necessary that the governor in council order the Anti-Inflation Board to study the potential inflationary impact of the groups to be affected and to report back.
The governor in council ordered the study on December 16, 1975. That was order No. P.C. 1975-2927, but it was never gazetted. That was one of the questions I wanted to put to the Minister of Finance in committee. Why was that order not published in the Canada Gazette? In any event, it was passed under what was alleged to be the authority of section 12(2) of the Anti-Inflation Act. Evidently the groups were found to be of strategic importance to the containment and reduction of

inflation in Canada. Those are the words of section 12(2) of the Anti-Inflation Act.
The study and recommendations were not published and appear to exist only as internal memoranda within the AIB itself. Surely we in the committee were entitled to ask for that memoranda and not to be cut off and guillotined by the majority Liberals on that committee, as happened on March 21.
The purpose of clause 1 is merely to give explicit legislative sanction to procedures already authorized by order in council. That must be clear. For reasons that are not completely clear, the government passed orders in council which by clause 1 the government wishes to confirm. No new procedures are authorized in clause 1. What is new is that the guidelines are made retroactive to December 16, 1975, whereas the order in council applied only from April 15, 1976. It is not clear who the government is trying to catch. Presumably there is a little black hole into which the government feels it must throw some people because of the inadvertence of the government with its order in council. I think this House has the right to know exactly who the government feels it is retroactively catching with the wording in clause 1, which is different from the wording in the order in council to which I have referred.
In any event, the Anti-Inflation Board advises that this change is a formality undertaken for the sake of uniformity and that no company or union will be required to give back profits or wages because of the new retroactive application. I hope the board is right, but surely in committee we were entitled to learn from the Minister of Finance what his answer would have been to that type of question. If clause 1 is of such small significance, one wonders why the Minister of Finance has chosen to trouble parliament with it. If the insertion of clause 1 was necessary to the legislative coherence of the program, why was it not necessary to insert it into Bill C-89 in the first instance? Why was it not put into Bill C-89?
Hon. members will recall that Bill C-89 was debated in April, 1976, the same month in which the order in council was proclaimed. The order in council was virtually identical to clause 1 of Bill C-18, the bill before us tonight. Apparently the administration did not wish parliament to debate this measure, although a ready opportunity existed when Bill C-89 was before the House. Delay in the debate of a measure like clause 1 clearly shows the reluctance of this administration to permit public debate on the anti-inflation program. That is one of the points I have been trying to bring out tonight.
This government-and I do not blame if-is obviously embarrassed by the failure of the anti-inflation program. However, whether it is embarrassed or not, it should be willing to make a complete reckoning to this House, and through this House to the Canadian public, as to why it has failed so miserably with its anti-inflation program.
Coming back to measures like clause 1, I think I should simply conclude by mentioning that de-control day was to be April 14, 1978. We must wonder whether the measure was really prompted because of the debate that the government anticipated would take place with regard to the utility of wage
April 3, 1978

and price controls themselves. Those are the references I wanted to make to clauses 1 and 8 as they appear in the bill which is now before us.
Let me now touch on clause 5 and clause 6. Some have called these the "ghost" amendments for decontrol. These amendments introduce a novel legal concept. The Anti-Inflation Act will expire by proclamation, presumably, on April 14, 1978. Incidentally, the only indication we have that decontrol will begin on April 14, 1978 is a comment made by the Prime Minister and reiterated on October 20 by the Minister of Finance. That is all we have. We have found that we cannot necessarily believe what these two gentlemen say, so how can we be absolutely sure that decontrol will begin on April 14? The fact is that to date that has never been proclaimed.
In any event, as I was saying, if the government sticks to its word, the anti-inflation program will presumably begin to be dismantled on April 14. Compliance with the terms of the act will, however, still be required in the sense that we have referred to the percentage dephasing month by month.
This brings me to the so-called ghost amendments which we find in clause 5 and clause 6 requiring compliance with a law which, if we believe the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, will no longer exist. Clause 5 makes extensive revisions to section 47 of the Anti-Inflation Act. Hon. members will recall that section 47 provides for the continuance of proceedings already instituted under the act, even though the act expired in the middle of the proceedings. The purpose of the section is to allow the completion of work under way by the Anti-Inflation Board, the administrator or the tribunal despite the termination of the act which gives these bodies authority to regulate wages and prices.
The amendment in clause 5 goes one step beyond the original section 47 by extending the powers of the board, the administrator or the tribunal to operate after the anti-inflation program has been legally terminated. Clause 5 would allow the Board to initiate proceedings after the legal end of controls for violations of the controls program which may have occurred while the controls were still in force. For example, if a company generates what is called excessive revenue during the final compliance period of the controls program, this amendment would allow the Anti-Inflation Board to investigate the revenue portion of the firm, find it to be in excess of the guidelines and order and enforce the distribution of the excess revenue of the firm.
The board, administrator or tribunal would have these powers-and I emphasize this-despite the fact that the act which gave them these powers will have expired. If we pass the bill which is now before us, that would be its effect, and let there be no doubt. These residual powers necessitate certain additional consequential amendments. Reporting requirements will remain in force. AIB staff will be retained. Vacancies on the board may be filled. All this may take place after the act has expired, perhaps as long as a full year thereafter.
On this particular point I am always taken aback by the number of people on the government side-in fact, including the chairman of the AIB himself-who are unaware of the
Anti-Inflation Act
fact that the present anti-inflation legislation can be extended beyond December 31, 1978 by a simple order of the cabinet.

speechtext:
If the Minister of Finance would care to look at the act he would find that the government can extend the termination of the AIB to whichever period it sees fit, subject to confirmation by the House at a later date. But the important thing that is often being forgotten is that this act does not automatically terminate on December 31 of this year. It can be extended by the government, and the only restraint on the government after it has extended the act is to be overruled by a vote in the House.
This brings me back to what I was saying that if, heaven forbid, this government should ever be returned with a majority, let there be no mistake; it will extend the AIB program, and if the House cares to have a vote on that program, the government will use its majority to push it through the House.
Let us bear in mind when considering Bill C-18 that the AIB will not necessarily end simply because the emperor, the Prime Minister, has said he thinks it should end by April 14. Also the Minister of Finance has said that, but both can reverse themselves. Believe me, political expediency is the only law this government obeys. Economic realities are secondary. If the government thinks it is politically expedient to tell us today that it intends to have a decontrol of the anti-inflation program, given re-election it will restore the controls program at the earliest opportunity.
Let me come back to clause 5. Clause 5 also attempts to invalidate the so-called AIB clauses in wage agreements. This was a deficiency pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) at a meeting of the committee. He was the first to make it clear that the legislation which the government brought in was defective. So clause 5 attempts to invalidate the so-called AIB clauses in wage settlements or, as it is sometimes referred to, there is a bounce back effect once the controls program ends with respect to any type of wage settlement that might have been higher than the guidelines.
Clause 6 also deals with wage agreements that have been reached calling for increases in compensation within the guidelines but which also specify that, after the termination of the controls programs, wages shall be paid at a rate considerably higher than would be allowed under the guidelines. Let me be a little clearer on that. For example, a 6 per cent wage agreement in force might provide for wages to be increased by a further 6 per cent once controls expire on whatever date is set. Clause 5(5) of Bill C-18 declares that such a provision would have no force or effect.
I suggest this measure is also a ghost clause. It requires compliance with the provisions of an act which will have expired, if we believe what the government is telling us.
Clause 6 also deals with wage agreements and is designed to prevent what has been called the bounce back of those wages, to which I have already referred. The bounce back would

April 3, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
occur because of the particular method used under the AntiInflation Act to control wages. If a wage agreement has been negotiated providing for an increase in compensation in excess of the guidelines, the AIB or the administrator rolls back what would then amount to an increase in excess of the guidelines. The actual roll-back procedure does not affect the wage agreement itself but only the amount which can be paid out under it. Suppose a compensation agreement calls for a 12 per cent increase in wages when only a 6 per cent increase is justified under the guidelines. The decision of the AIB, or the ruling of the administrator, specifies that a 6 per cent increase only may be paid out. The decision or ruling does not, I emphasize, alter the terms of the contract itself. Thus, when the Anti-Inflation Act expires and the AIB ceases to exist, the original contract would immediately become payable at the old rate or, in the example I have given, at 12 per cent. Further, companies might be required to pay retroactively wages lost due to the AIB limit on the pay out of the settlement.
Clause 6 states that a ruling of the AIB or the administrator actually modifies the terms of the contract so that it will comply with the guidelines. This is not merely a ghost clause, as the "deemed modification" of a contract will take place while the Anti-Inflation Act is still in force, although the effect of the modification will be felt even after the act has expired. In conjunction with clause 5, clause 6 should prevent any attempt by a union or a company to exceed the guidelines while the compensation agreement is in force.
However, and this is the point, there is nothing in either clause 5 or clause 6 which will prevent a union and company agreeing to terminate a contract when the act expires. Once terminated, a new contract could be negotiated comparatively free of any guidelines.
The ghost amendments are a legal oddity and it is difficult to predict how effective they will be. Fortunately, they are only transitional powers for the decontrol period. One hopes that the administration will resist further attempts to create legal obligations pursuant to such non-existent laws. The ghost amendments show how much easier it is to start controls than to end them.
Having reviewed Bill C-18 and some aspects of the antiinflation program to the point that I have at this time, let me point out that surely the Prime Minister was right when he made that famous statement that controls are a disaster looking for a place to happen. Do you recall that, Mr. Speaker? In fact, controls are not something that effectively control inflation-they cause problems. The Prime Minister had it right. Now unfortunately we have had inflicted upon us a controls program which, as I said earlier, has resulted in higher inflation in Canada than our main trading partners have experienced, certainly higher than in the United States. Yet we are being asked tonight, without, I suggest, having had a proper opportunity to review this legislation in the committee, to pass Bill C-18 relatively quickly, and without the explanation from the Minister of Finance to which I believe we are entitled.
This brings me to an interesting question when we are considering the anti-inflation position of the government. How often will we be subjected to the rhetoric we get from the government on what they propose and intend to do with respect to certain matters such as inflation? All we are left with is rhetoric but no action. I refer to this because already I have made reference to a letter written by the Prime Minister to Dr. Ostry in which he set out the terms of reference he would like her to follow in carrying out the monitoring of inflation starting on April 14.
There was also a letter sent by the Prime Minister to what were called business and labour leaders, which was dated July 29, 1977. In the letter the government set out what it regarded as an appropriate decontrol and post-control arrangement. The letter had many paragraphs in it, 15 I believe. In paragraph 8 it was stated that the government hoped to establish what they called a multipartite consultative forum and monitoring agency. This has been described in "Agenda for Co-operation", a copy of which I have here. The Prime Minister stated at that time:
These have been described in Agenda for Co-operation. In more specific terms, it is now proposed that the consultative forum should be constituted as follows.
This is the form he was proposing less than a year ago. He indicated that there should be ten participants from business, of whom at least five would be selected from a list of ten nominations by the business council on national issues. It would have ten participants from labour, of whom six would be selected in consultation with the Canadian Labour Congress. Five participants would come from interested groups, and five would be federal government ministers.
In item 9 of his letter he stated that, in selecting the participants, the government would ensure an appropriate balance with respect to industrial sectors and regions. In item No. 10 he stated that in selecting the board of the monitoring agency, the government would ensure that people of stature with a recognized experience in business and labour would be included.
On October 20 last year the Minister of Finance referred to those clauses before the House, yet we have heard nothing further. We have received no explanation from the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister as to why the proposals were not carried out.

Perhaps that is the best evidence we have received as to where the entire program has gone wrong. It may be administered by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). If that is so, it should have been made clear much earlier, and then we could have directed our questions to the Minister of National Defence. I was not aware that "Minister of National Defence" meant "defence against inflation", or whatever interpretation the minister places upon it. I do not mean to be critical of the jolly Minister of National Defence. He is a neighbouring member of parliament to my

April 3, 1978

riding. He is a jolly good fellow. If he was made Minister of Finance, I would hope he would do a much better job in that portfolio than he has done as Minister of National Defence. Certainly he could not do a worse job than the present Minister of Finance.
Perhaps we will receive a little more insight bit by bit from the ministers as to who has the truth. Now I have learned that we should have directed questions concerning the anti-inflation program to the Minister of National Defence, to that degree a little progress has been made this evening.
I should like to know what happened concerning this letter of July 29. At that time it sounded somewhat interesting. An illustrious emperor was going forth and stating, in a letter addressed to labour and business leaders, what he would like to see happen. Well, what happened? Where was he turned down? Are we to accept that the Economic Council of Canada is what he had in mind? If that is so, we must remember that the labour component of the Economic Council dropped away. They decided they did not want to participate any longer in the Economic Council. Clearly there is no labour participation in the Economic Council.
I raise these points, and in particular this letter, during the debate on Bill C-18 because we should have been entitled to ask the part-time Minister of Finance in committee what happened to those proposals. Was it the government's decision to drop them? Was it labour or business? Who exactly said "scrap that letter, the idea is no good"? I could refer to various sections of that letter, but I should like to indicate that the 15 clauses set out have never been heard from since. Perhaps the Minister of National Defence has been having secret meetings with business and labour leaders. Perhaps he is the man who runs the anti-inflation program. As far as we have been able to make out, no meetings have taken place. The government has not met with labour, business or consumer groups. In short, the government is getting ready for an election. They are hoping to bamboozle the Canadian public and ensure re-election when they decide to go to the country. If that is the intention of the government, it is very, very important for its performance with respect to inflation to be put on the record clearly.
The policies of the Trudeau government have placed this nation solidly in the grip of inflation on a relatively permanent basis. The current annual rate of inflation is 9.5 per cent. That rate means prices in this country will double every eight years if it is permitted to continue. Because of the ineptitude of the government, it will continue at some comparable level should the government be allowed to continue running the financial management of Canada. Every hon. member must accept the basic premise that inflation is created by the Bank of Canada through the excess printing of money in relation to our real growth. The government is aware of that. As long as that is tolerated, the consequences must be accepted. One of those consequences is high inflation.
High inflation is nothing new to the Trudeau government. Actually, prices have risen by 87 per cent since our Prime Minister took office. That is according to the consumer price
Anti-Inflation Act
index. If one looks at the deflator, or the implicit price index, one will find that prices have gone up 100 per cent. That 100 per cent increase is 13 per cent higher than what the CPI reflects. In the main it is government inflation which is reflected in the deflator. That has gone up even faster than the rate of price increases as reflected by the CPI.
When the government's record on inflation is considered, the broken promises regarding inflation should be noted. The Trudeau government announced that it had defeated inflation on several occasions, only to have it return with a vengeance. In December 1970 the Prime Minister crowed the following: "Inflation no longer exists in Canada". Since then, prices have risen by 72 per cent. When the Prime Minister campaigned against wage and price controls in 1974, the "emperor" then said: "We are going to bring inflation under control. That I pledge to you". That pledge has brought price increases of 35 per cent since then.
The litany of failure to bring inflation under control continues to the present day. In October, 1975, the Liberal administration introduced the wage and price controls which they campaigned against in 1974. This fact is well known. The controls program presented targets for inflation from a level of 10.6 per cent in October, 1975. The rate of inflation was forecast to fall to 8 per cent by October 1976, to 6 per cent by October, 1977, and to 4 per cent by October, 1978.
The 1978 target was achieved when the inflation rate stood at 6.2 per cent in October. One year later, however, the inflation rate had increased to 8.8 per cent, well over the target of 6 per cent. Although the Trudeau government promised 4 per cent inflation in 1978, it has reneged on that commitment and now forecasts 6 per cent inflation this year. My guess is that it will soon abandon that target as well. The fact is that at the present time the Minister of Finance, and possibly his emperor friend, are the only people in Canada who still seriously believe there will be 6 per cent inflation in this country in the current year.
What about the 1978 inflation prospects? Our minister has forecast 6 per cent inflation in 1978. Many private sector forecasters think this is unrealistic. The Conference Board of Canada expects inflation to average 7.4 per cent in 1978. In that respect I note that the Minister of Finance often quotes the Chairman of that Board, particularly since he decided to run as a candidate for this party.
The Bank of Commerce expects 7.8 per cent inflation this year; the Bank of British Columbia predicts 7.9 per cent and Levesque, Beaubien, Incorporated in Quebec expects 7.8 per cent inflation. Even the government's own advisory agency, the Economic Council of Canada, which the government has asked to monitor inflation, expects inflation to average 7.4 per cent in 1978.
What are the inflationary pressures? We know wholesale prices are 10.9 per cent higher at this time than a year ago. Adding to inflation are two further pressures on prices in

April 3, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
Canada. I refer, of course, to the continuing fall of the dollar and our higher energy prices.
In the area of food costs, the impact of our falling dollar is already apparent. Higher import prices will continue to push up consumer prices. Canadian manufacturers who use imports in production face higher costs. Canadian corporations which have borrowed funds in foreign currencies will be required to pay much higher repayment costs.
In that connection, it has been estimated that the total foreign borrowings of Canadians, be they municipalities, corporations, provincial or federal governments, are approximately $33 billion. It does not take much of a mathematician to figure out that if you have a 10 per cent decline in the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to those currencies you have borrowed you will be losing $3.3 billion should you have to repay those foreign currencies with a falling Canadian dollar.
On that particular point-and I am pleased the Minister of Finance is here-I hope that before this debate ends he will explain to the House what his government expects to do to relieve the plight of the municipalities, corporations and provinces which, at the government's behest, went out and borrowed in foreign funds and are now left with considerably higher monetary amounts to pay than first anticipated, directly as a result of the government's current decision to allow the dollar to fall. I was going to say "allow the government to fall", which would be a blessing, Mr. Speaker.
Let me put that into another time frame. It could cost $3.3 billion in extra payout on the part of those who borrowed foreign funds if they have to pay off their debts in terms of Canada's fallen dollar. One must think of the interest cost as well, because most of those obligations were expressed not only in respect of capital, but in respect of the interest on foreign currencies. The debt or interest payments will also be 10 per cent higher than anticipated. There should be some indication from the government about its intent to relieve that situation. Does the government intend to leave those municipalities, corporations, and provinces in effect holding the bag because they acted in response to the government's request to go out and seek foreign funds at a time when the government was desperately trying to hold up the Canadian dollar? The dollar would have fallen in any event because our trade imbalance was already running at an alarmingly high level.
One other point I should touch upon is that we are very conscious of the effect of a falling dollar in relation to import prices. However, I was most surprised at a committee meeting to find that the Minister of Finance and his advisers were not as conscious of the effect of a falling dollar in relation to various commodities within Canada. I refer specifically to the price of some Canadian goods such as beef and lumber. The prices of both those commodities are quoted to Canadian buyers in terms of the U.S. dollar equivalent. As a result, to the extent you have a falling dollar you automatically ensure that domestically in Canada the price of beef, lumber and other commodities will go up. Hopefully the Minister of Finance will come forward and explain why this government feels the falling dollar is such a desirable thing when it will

have such an impact, not only on the price of imports to this country, but also on the price Canadians will have to pay for such commodities as beef, lumber and others.
Dealing with this broad subject of the inflationary pressures we will experience this year, the federal Department of Finance has estimated that the recent devaluation of the dollar could add 4 per cent to our inflation rate within two years. The government will increase the domestic price of oil and natural gas twice during the year, each time by one dollar per barrel or its natural gas equivalent. The immediate impact of the price change will be felt in home heating and automobile fuel. The two price changes alone will raise the consumer price index by 1 per cent by the year end. Oil and gas used by consumer goods producers will result in higher consumer prices. Energy costs account for between 5 per cent and 10 per cent of farm production costs. The 1978 energy price increases may increase, if we follow that through, consumer goods by 1 per cent or more. These are some of the pressures we are facing in relation to inflation during 1978.
Let me touch on one question which is perhaps more important during this debate than any other. What causes inflation? The blame for inflation has been laid at almost everyone's doorstep. I mentioned earlier that the government liked to say that labour, business or foreign countries were to blame. Do hon. members remember when we had that minister of finance, two or three back, by the name of Mr. Turner? He used to come into the House when he was embarrassed about inflation and say that because anchovies off the coast of South America had gone wrong-somehow or other they could not find them-it meant we had higher inflation in Canada. At other times we have been told inflation was caused by the financial gnomes in Zurich who were manipulating the system. We were even told there were mysterious cartels at work which somehow or other caused inflation. It later became brutally clear that this government had set up a cartel in respect of uranium, the like of which the world had never seen before. As a result this will cost Ontario consumers, and presumably other consumers in Canada, additional hundreds of millions of dollars. It does not matter who the government pretends is responsible for inflation; the fact is that inflation could not and would not occur unless the government either encouraged, or permitted it, and that is the simple truth. Not only the Minister of Finance but the emperor himself have consistently encouraged inflation and permitted it. Inflation is always caused by government. It is the government which controls the supply of money, and it is excess money which causes inflation.
This brings me back to the falling Canadian dollar. The interesting thing that has happened is that while the government has been acting so irresponsibly with respect to inflation, they to a certain degree were getting away with it so long as other governments acted equally as irresponsible. However, there has been a sobering influence in the world. Countries such as Germany and Switzerland, and Japan to a lesser extent, have decided they are going to stop the excess printing
April 3, 1978

of money as far as the economy is concerned. They have said they are going to get a handle on inflation and in short are not going to play the game of printing more money and living with inflation any longer. The result is that our big spending friends on the other side have been caught off base because they now find that the game has changed and that they no longer can spend as excessively as originally. The government can no longer print money as excessively as they were because countries such as Germany, Japan and Switzerland are not doing it.
To the degree that this government has failed to be equally as responsible, we find that international investors have been moving away from our dollar to invest in the German Deutschmark, the Swiss franc or the Japanese yen. That is what is happening, and let there be no pretence of anything else. In the eyes of the world, we are one of the weak currencies today, and to the degree that the international investor looks upon Canada as a weak nation, the run will continue so long as they look on the German, the Swiss or the Japanese currencies as stronger. The run will continue from our currency to that type of more solid currency.
I think it is important when we are considering this amendment to the government's Anti-Inflation Act that we virtually insist that the Minister of Finance get up and give an explanation as to why as were told in October, 1975 that the government have a program to handle inflation and yet we find that we still have no answers.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance is saying that he thinks I am taking too long. To what extent, Mr. Speaker, am I entitled to time? I was not given the right to put questions in the finance committee. Surely if there are points that have not been made by the minister or his cohorts concerning this anti-inflation program, members of this House have the right to speak and ask what they feel fit.
Let me come back to the main point that I want to make, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the government can control inflation. As an example, suppose a customer has $100 to spend and he normally spends $25 on each of food, energy, housing and clothing. If the price of energy, for example, should double, he must either buy less energy or less of something else. The only way he can continue to buy the same amount of goods as before is if he increases his supply of money. It is the same with government and with the Canadian economy. An increase in the price of oil or an increase in wages or profits is not inflationary unless more money is printed at the same time. If the supply of money remains the same, an increase in the national price of oil simply causes people to spend less on other items. If the pie remains the same size, a larger slice for one group means a smaller slice for other groups. Individual price, profits or wage increases are redistributed in their effect and are only inflationary if the government tries to stop the redistribution by increasing the supply of money. By trying to cancel the effect of price and wage changes through increasing the supply of money, the government only provokes others to restore their share. More money
Anti-Inflation Act
in the system does not necessarily make the pie any larger. It just makes it more expensive to buy.
When the federal government lives beyond its means, one of the ways it pays for its deficits is by selling securities to the Bank of Canada, and it in turn pays for the securities by printing money. This is inflation in its most direct form. The government should not finance deficits or even try to ease the shock of a particular price increase by an increase in the money supply. Stimulated monetary policies are not necessarily inflationary, and the money supply should always expand in relation to the actual size of the economy.
It must be made clear that inflation cannot occur unless it is permitted to occur by an expansion of the money supply. The relationship of monetary growth to inflation is clear. From the winter of 1968 to the late fall of 1977 the money supply increased by 156 per cent. I hope you will pay particular attention, Mr. Speaker, to the figures that I am giving. Between that period this government printed 156 per cent more money in Canada. Over the same period real economic growth was 55 per cent. The difference between the two, 101 per cent, represents the amount of money created in excess of that required to finance the growth in the economy. It is no surprise, therefore, to discover that the general price level in the economy increased by 100 per cent in the same period, almost exactly the same as the amount of excess money printed.
Let us note those figures again, Mr. Speaker. In the period from late 1968 to the fall of 1977 the government caused the Bank of Canada to grind out 156 per cent more money supply in the nation. During the same period the real growth was only 55 per cent, so they created in excess of 101 per cent as far as the money supply is concerned. Our inflation when you use the deflator was exactly 100 per cent during that period, within one per cent of the excess money created during this government's reign of office.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker, and when we are considering amendments to the anti-inflation legislation, Bill C-18, the government should explain why they continuously pretend that they need monitoring agencies, that they need controls, that they are not too sure what is causing inflation when, simply, they are printing the inflation that we are living on.
I would like to touch on the historical perspective of this situation. A large proportion of the money printed in recent years has gone to finance the Trudeau government's deficits. The Bank of Canada has printed money to finance 33 per cent of the federal cash requirements in the past five years. The $5.6 billion of federal securities purchased by the Bank of Canada represents more than 60 per cent of the total addition to the money supply over that period.
