subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INCLUSION IN BUDGET OF INCENTIVES FOR VOLUNTARY WORK-SHARING
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INCLUSION IN BUDGET OF INCENTIVES FOR VOLUNTARY WORK-SHARING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to listen to a monologist explaining his simple theories in a very complex world.
I believe that at this point we are in the middle of an international economic crisis with the problems that most countries have to face. Techniques are not working, particularly techniques which clearly should create jobs and increase demand. Those particular techniques do not work and have not been working as they used to. A good example of this is that, although we have put $4.5 billion or so on the demand side of our economy in the last 15 months, we have not been able to solve the problem of creating employment. In addition, we have serious energy problems which make for greater economic problems.
Because of the baby boom in the 1950s and early 1960s, Canada is experiencing a very large growth in the labour force. About 300,000 young people come on the labour market each year, or about four or five times the number that came on the labour market in the 1950's. These problems create some very serious distortions in the economy and create unemployment at the rate of 8 or 9 per cent. In the age group 15 to 24, unemployment is in the area of 14 or 15 per cent.
Because it is very difficult to create jobs, given the fact that demand and other techniques do not work and respond the way they used to, we have to look at methods of reorganizing the job market. I am particularly concerned with the failure of our experts to increase the number of jobs available. The rate of growth in the United States in the first quarter of this year is most disturbing-it is actually a zero growth rate. Given this kind of problem, it seems to me we must do something far more significant in terms of job creation or putting a large number of people into the work force.
One method we might look at is this. If we cannot create additional jobs, then the amount of work available could in some way or other be shared among the people available to do it. I should like to look at work sharing and the possibilities of voluntary work sharing as a partial solution to some of the problems which face us. I know there is already some worksharing, especially when plants have lay-offs, but it seems to me a large number of people who are working would voluntarily adopt some form of work-sharing. This could be pairing, shorter weeks and so on. The reward, of course, would be the extra leisure time. I think this is particularly the case in professions such as teaching and nursing where pairing is

worth-while. Many people would like half the work-load by taking half a day's work each, or working a week at a time, for instance.
Some problems are involved in work-sharing but one of the advantages, particularly with pairing, is that the productivity of the two individuals involved is usually higher than the productivity of one person doing the job full time. Other problems concern benefits, incentives, extra clerical work required by the employer for pay-rolls and so on.
These are some things that could and should be looked at by this government. I ask the minister to look seriously at incentives which would have the effect of overcoming some of the objections to work sharing. I would like the government to take on a program of attempting to get Canadians to volunteer to share the work they have with those Canadians who cannot find work. In that way we would not have one large group of people on the labour market, working eight hours a day for 40 years, with another group not working at all. I know there are regional problems and so on, but that would be a partial solution.
With the government coming out with a new budget within the next month or so, I hope it will seriously look at incentives to share the amount of work available among the people available to do it.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST WAR DISABILITY PENSION BE RAISED TO LEVEL OF 1973 FORMULA
VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST WAR DISABILITY PENSION BE RAISED TO LEVEL OF 1973 FORMULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 17, as reported in Hansard at page 3872, I put two questions to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). One of them had to do with the basic rate of the war disability pension and the other with the formula which determines when a disabled veteran's widow will get a pension following the death of her husband.
As the minister knows, and as the House knows, I put these two questions to the minister as often as I can. Indeed, earlier this afternoon I sought to present a motion under Standing Order 43 dealing with these two issues. Until not many weeks ago my questions about veterans affairs were three. In addition to my plea that something be done about the basic rate and the formula respecting widows, I was calling for amendments to
Adjournment Debate
the legislation respecting compensation for prisoners of war. As the minister knows, not only did he win his battle in cabinet and obtain agreement to bring in a bill extending compensation to prisoners of war of the first world war and also to evaders and escapers in the second world war, but he also won that legislation on the floor of the House in a matter of two or three hours; the bill went through all its stages on the same day.
I remind the minister of this because I should like to impress upon him, as I did when I questioned him on March 17, that he could do it again. If he brings in a measure improving the legislation affecting our veterans I can guarantee that the House will give it approval in a very short period of time. Speaking of time, we all know there is not much of it left for this session or, indeed, for this parliament. Surely the minister would like to go into an election campaign knowing that this legislation has been passed instead of having a record which says, time after time, only that the matter is under consideration. I would remind him that the convention of the Royal Canadian Legion may be held right in the middle of the election campaign, and though he may be busy in Prince Edward Island I suspect he will be invited to that convention. When he gets there he will find that two foremost issues will be those I am bringing forward tonight-the question of the basic rate and of the formula which applies to the widows of veterans.
With respect to the basic rate, the facts are well known to all concerned. Back in 1973 a formula was agreed to which called for the rate to be set so that the amount available for a 100 per cent disabled veteran would be equal to the average take-home pay of five categories in the federal public service. The hope was that this formula would carry through. Instead, although the rate was set in 1973 the increase each year has been only in accordance with the rise in the consumer price index and the basic rate has fallen behind.
It is true that the 7.2 per cent increase in January of this year narrowed the gap slightly. I received a letter only today informing me that the gap was now down to $311 a year. But I would remind the minister that this year's increase for the public service has not yet come through and no doubt when it does the gap will be back to $500 or $600 a year.
This is an issue on which there are strong feelings from coast to coast. I am making a plea to the minister. But I am also giving him a tremendous opportunity. He is going into an election campaign. He is going to a meeting of the Canadian Legion. Why not come through with this restoration of the basic rate to the amount that would be calculated by the formula agreed to in 1973?
I make the same offer to the minister with respect to widows. In fact, it would not surprise me if, when the Legion convention is held, those who take the resolutions before that convention will give very high priority to this question of widows. As veterans get older and more and more of them realize that their pensions are below 48 per cent and that their

April 3, 1978
Adjournment Debate
wives will not get a pension if the veteran dies first, they are concerned about this provision. It still just does not make sense to say that when a wife looks after her veteran husband who is on a 48 per cent pension and he dies first she gets a full widow's pension, but if the wife next door is looking after a veteran who is on a 47 per cent pension or anything less, she gets no pension at all. To say she can fall back on the war veterans allowance really does not answer the point.
I appreciate the fact that the minister has stayed here for the late show tonight. If he is looking for something new from me, I have to reply that there is nothing new to say on these two issues. We have been over them time and time again. The something new is in the minister's hands. The something new is for the minister to get up tonight and not just say that they are under consideration but to say that he shares my hope and the hope of all members of this House that these two issues will be acted on by the government and by parliament before this session ends.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST WAR DISABILITY PENSION BE RAISED TO LEVEL OF 1973 FORMULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his continuing concern for the wellbeing of our veteran population and their dependants. The hon. member knows that the question of increasing the basic rate of disability pension has been discussed in this House several times in the last few months. Disability pensions were increased by 7.2 per cent on January 1 of this year. The basic rate for an unmarried 100 per cent pensioner is $596.70 a month. If that pensioner is married, the amount is $745.88 a month, and if he and his wife have two dependent children, his pension is $880.15 per month.
I have said that I intend to have the government consider the possibility of raising the basic rate again, and when I have something to report to the House on this subject, I shall be pleased to do so.
The hon. member suggests that a widow should receive a pro rata pension if her husband had been in receipt of a disability pension of 47 per cent or less. This is because she would receive a widow's pension if his pension had been 48 per cent or more at the time of his death. It was decided that a veteran receiving a 48 per cent or more pension would have been disabled to the degree that his disability would have contributed to his early death. It should be remembered that a widow will be pensioned if her husband's death occurred during wartime or was attributable to his service, regardless of the degree of the assessment of his disability.
Canada continues to be a world leader in providing benefits to disabled veterans and their dependants. I know of no other country that pays automatic survivor benefits to widows approaching the 48 per cent basis that we in Canada use.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL ENGAGED IN SEARCH FOR REMAINS OF SOVIET SATELLITE
NATIONAL DEFENCE-ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL ENGAGED IN SEARCH FOR REMAINS OF SOVIET SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 1, as recorded at page 2438 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) if the armed services person-

nel stationed at Churchill were involved in searching for the satellite which came down in the Northwest Territories. At that time I was appalled by the remarks made by the minister. He said he had been up to the Northwest Territories, and he told us of the very harsh conditions in the Northwest Territories under which the armed forces personnel had to work. I pointed out that there are thousands of people in the Northwest Territories who work in these conditions day in and day out.
That brings me to the reason I have raised this matter in the adjournment debate tonight. Over the last 25 years Churchill has become a very important area for winter warfare training. I believe Churchill is the most appropriate location for winter warfare training because there is tundra just north of Churchill, the tree line is just to the south of Churchill and there are ideal training conditions.
Over the past few years we have seen a total erosion of the involvement of the armed services and of the Department of National Defence in Churchill. Fort Churchill was built in 1946; now it has been almost totally demolished. There are only 35 armed services families left there. There is concern that these 35 families will be slowly transferred out of Churchill and that the fort will be almost completely dismantled, which will mean that no one from the armed services will be left in that location.
Let us take a look at the geographic location of Churchill, the excellent airport facilities and storage buildings there, etc. Fort Churchill is the most northerly point along the Hudson Bay coast and into the Arctic, and it is an essential location from which to protect our northern frontier. I do not understand why the government, instead of training personnel in winter warfare in other locations where northern conditions must be simulated, does not put more emphasis on relocating the armed forces personnel in Churchill.
In 1946 when the army was first located in Churchill, the town was built up to a point where approximately 5,000 people were living in Churchill between the fort and the town site. Now that the fort has been dismantled, a $50 million resettlement plan was set up for the Churchill town site which involved moving all the facilities from the fort.
At the same time the CBC is pulling out of Churchill at the end of June, which will mean that only 12 CBC people will be left there. Also, the National Research Council will pull out of Churchill, as I understand, because, as they say, it is too expensive for them to remain there. That will leave only two NRC families in Churchill. The space program is to be continued but people will move from Gimli to Churchill for the rocket launches and then back to Gimli.
I am glad to see the minister here tonight because it is very important to the people of Churchill and, I believe, to the whole of Canada to have an active and effective winter warfare training element in a place like Churchill. A further erosion of the presence of armed forces in Churchill will mean that a community where a $50 million redevelopment program
April 3, 1978

has been commenced will decrease to the point where it will number some 1,200 people only. First there was the building up of a community from 1946 onward until the tearing down of the fort in 1976. Then there was a redevelopment and rebuilding of the town. Now the federal government is slowly pulling out its services from that community. This is another blatant example of lack of government planning.
There is an $11 million recreation complex being built in the town of Churchill as part of the redevelopment program. This complex is serving now some 15,000 people only. It is like an albatross, around the necks of the people in Churchill amounting to about $8,000 a year, which the maintenance of this complex is costing them. Churchill does not have a big enough tax base to support such a complex. The population of Churchill is faced with actually locking the doors on it if there is to be an erosion of government involvement there. It is the government in the first place that made the main decision for the redevelopment because the federal government paid the lion's share for it.
I ask the minister to give serious consideration to retaining a good size core of armed services personnel in Churchill. It provides an excellent opportunity. There is not another place in Canada where winter warfare training can be simulated any better. A unit such as that would be very beneficial in searching for a satellite which has come down, though I hope that never happens again. The troops would be accustomed to the climate and conditions and would be able to step in because they have taken their daily training in that area.
Also I should like to mention I was very disappointed to see the Thompson application for a militia was turned down. This ties in with the fact that the number of armed services people in Churchill is diminishing. We want to see a little more involvement by the Department of National Defence in the north to protect our frontiers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL ENGAGED IN SEARCH FOR REMAINS OF SOVIET SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the comments of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith). I appreciate he is aware of the tremendous investment the federal government has made already in Churchill. I hope in the long run that will pay off. Particularly I was interested in his comments regarding its suitability as a winter warfare training centre. The hon.
Adjournment Debate
member is quite right; the conditions of the Arctic can be simulated there.
The units which participated in the search for the downed satellite were not from Churchill. I am sure many of the people who were involved received their Arctic training in the Churchill area. This area is certainly considered a valuable training area. It does not lend itself to the large infrastructure required by the nature of the training. One difficulty is that there are a variety of different types of Arctic conditions. Our troops are training in different parts of the Arctic. When they move there, they are there to survive in that very rugged atmosphere. One of the good things is that there is an opportunity for relaxation in Churchill because of the excellent facilities which have been provided. I know the sports and recreation complexes to which the hon. member referred.
We must look at the broad picture of where we receive the most value and best return for the investment in infrastructure which we have. That is done automatically on a continuing basis to see that taxpayers' money is being handled properly in the first place, and that we are using the facilities to their best potential. Certainly Churchill offers a potential, but it does not lend itself to the large type of infrastructure of other places because of the nature of the training. The troops are on the road and away from the base itself, but they are necessary to maintain minimum facilities. I am sure the hon. member realizes that, as he also realizes the value of that training to the Canadian armed forces.
With regard to the other point about other government departments, I am not in a position to comment, nor is it appropriate for me to comment, on the Thompson situation with reference to the Cameron Highlanders. We are not talking about pulling out any who are there, but it is something which has been under consideration. In so far as Churchill is concerned, there are no immediate plans for any changes there. The value of the area for Arctic warfare training is appreciated. Our troops go there on their own and maintain themselves in that quite rugged environment. It is that type of training which has made our troops among the best in the world in Arctic and winter warfare.
